00How to Use This Playbook

This is a living reference, not a script to memorize. As a new SDR, use it to build foundational knowledge about Trimble, our customers, and the outbound motion. As you gain experience, come back to individual sections when you're planning a territory, sharpening messaging, or coaching yourself through a rough patch. Managers can lean on it during onboarding, 1:1s, and role plays to keep expectations consistent across the team.

As Trimble's products, markets, and go-to-market strategy evolve, this guide evolves with them. See the Change Log for version history.

PART I

The Outbound SDR Role

01Welcome to the Trimble AECO Outbound SDR Team

As an Outbound SDR, you play a critical role in helping organizations discover new ways to improve how they design, build, and operate the world's infrastructure. Every conversation you start has the potential to uncover a business challenge, introduce a new perspective, and create an opportunity that helps a customer transform how they work.

Inbound customers have already raised a hand. Outbound customers haven't — which means success here comes from initiative, research, and persistence rather than speed and triage. It takes curiosity, thoughtful preparation, personalized outreach, and the ability to build trust with people who don't yet realize there's a better way to solve their problem. (Section 2 gets into exactly how this differs from inbound.)

This playbook reflects how we sell at Trimble: the goal was never just booking meetings. It's creating business conversations that help customers solve problems they may not have fully named yet.

What This Playbook Covers

Over time, this guide will build out how to understand your role within the Trimble sales org, build territory and account plans, research target accounts and buying committees, develop industry expertise, run personalized multi-channel outreach, conduct real discovery, qualify opportunities, partner with your AE, use technology and AI well, and measure your own performance. It doesn't replace manager coaching, product training, or methodology courses — it's the practical layer that ties those together for day-to-day work.

Why Outbound Matters at Trimble

The most valuable opportunities aren't always the ones that come to us. Many organizations that would benefit most from Trimble's solutions haven't filled out a form or requested a demo — they're heads-down running projects, managing teams, and hitting deadlines. Outbound lets us reach these organizations before they've started a buying journey, surfacing opportunities to improve efficiency, reduce risk, and modernize how they work before a competitor gets there first.

Done well, this expands Trimble into new markets and accounts, builds relationships with future customers, and generates the qualified pipeline the business is forecasting against. Every new outbound conversation is a potential first chapter of a long-term customer relationship.

The Outbound SDR's Role in Revenue Creation

Rather than responding to existing demand, you're generating it — through research, outreach, and conversations that wouldn't have happened otherwise. That means holding several roles at once:

RoleWhat It Means Day to Day
Territory StrategistUnderstand your assigned territory, identify whitespace, prioritize target accounts, and build a long-term pipeline plan with your AE
Industry SpecialistDevelop real expertise in the industries you support so your outreach is relevant and credible, not generic
Business ResearcherResearch companies, initiatives, stakeholders, and buying signals to personalize outreach and spot where Trimble creates value
Trusted AdvisorApproach every conversation with curiosity — ask, listen, and understand the business before discussing solutions
AE PartnerBuild account strategy together, coordinate outreach, share insight, and create opportunities that actually move

What Success Looks Like

Consistency in outreach matters, but it's not the differentiator — execution quality is. High-performing Outbound SDRs consistently build strategic account plans, prioritize the right opportunities, research before engaging, personalize across channels, ask insightful discovery questions, qualify effectively, hand off cleanly to their AE, keep CRM data accurate, and keep learning. Success is measured by the quality of the conversations and the pipeline they generate — not the number of activities logged.

What's Expected of You

Think strategically about your territory instead of working it reactively. Lead with curiosity instead of assumptions. Personalize every interaction — customers can tell when they haven't been researched. Execute with discipline; the fundamentals done consistently beat occasional bursts of activity. Collaborate as one team with your AE, fellow SDRs, and Marketing. Own your own development instead of waiting to be told what to improve. And put the customer first: before any outreach, conversation, or recommendation, ask yourself, "how can I create value for this customer?" Section 3 goes deep on the mindset behind each of these — this is just the preview.

Some of your conversations will turn into opportunities right away. Others will plant something that develops six months or a year from now. Either way, you're not just the first step in the sales process — you're the beginning of the customer relationship. Show up prepared, professional, and curious, and the relationships you build today become the pipeline Trimble runs on tomorrow.

02Understanding the Outbound Motion

Outbound customers aren't shopping for software — they're running their business, and many don't yet know a better way of working exists. That means your job isn't to schedule meetings; it's to create awareness, earn trust, and start conversations that otherwise never would have happened. It takes patience and preparation, and every interaction should create value whether or not it leads to a meeting this week.

Inbound vs. Outbound

Both motions build pipeline, but the mechanics are different enough that treating outbound like "inbound, but colder" doesn't work.

Inbound SDROutbound SDR
Responds to customer interestCreates customer interest
Customer has already engagedCustomer may have no prior engagement
Focuses on speed and qualificationFocuses on research and relationship building
Converts demand into opportunityGenerates demand through proactive outreach
Shorter path to discoveryLonger path to engagement

Neither motion outranks the other — together they produce a balanced, predictable pipeline.

Creating Demand, Not Manufacturing It

Creating demand means helping customers recognize an opportunity they hadn't fully considered — not convincing them they have a problem they don't. In practice, that's sharing a relevant industry insight, asking a genuinely good business question, or connecting an operational headache to a business outcome, with more curiosity than pitch. The interest comes from the conversation being valuable, not from a well-produced deck.

Pipeline Gets Built One Conversation at a Time

Every outbound opportunity moves through the same sequence: pick the right account, research the business, form a hypothesis about their priorities, identify the stakeholders, personalize the outreach, follow up consistently, run real discovery, qualify, and partner with your AE on the handoff. Skipping a step — usually research, in a rush to send the email — is the most common reason engagement is low.

Today's Buyer Has Already Done Homework

Before an SDR ever reaches them, most prospects have already researched potential solutions, compared vendors, read reviews, and talked to peers. That means you earn attention by adding something they don't already have — not by introducing yourself. Conversations land when they're relevant, personalized, timely, tied to business outcomes, and respectful of the person's time. Approach every interaction as helping, not selling.

Enterprise Buying Is a Team Sport

Trimble's Outbound SDRs support both Mid-Market and Enterprise New Logo AEs, where deals routinely involve executive sponsors, business leaders, operational users, technical evaluators, procurement, and finance. Don't assume one good conversation equals one decision. Work with your AE to map the broader buying committee and look for chances to engage more than one stakeholder over time.

Multi-Threading

Organizations decide collectively, and different stakeholders weigh different things. As you work an account, keep track of who actually experiences the problem, who owns the budget, who influences the decision, who will use the solution day to day, and who signs off on the investment. A single-threaded relationship — one contact, no matter how friendly — is the most common reason a promising opportunity stalls when that person goes quiet or changes roles.

Industry Expertise Changes the Conversation

Trimble's Outbound SDR org is aligned by industry — Civil, MEP, General Contracting, Structures, or ERP Cross-sell — specifically so reps can develop real fluency instead of generic messaging. Each of these has different priorities, workflows, technology ecosystems, buying triggers, and personas, and speaking that specific language is what makes an unsolicited email feel credible instead of like spam. As industry-specific playbook chapters get built out, they'll live alongside this one.

It's a Process, Not an Event

Very few opportunities come from a single email or call. A real outbound motion combines personalized emails, phone conversations, LinkedIn engagement, relevant follow-up content, account research, and ongoing coordination with your AE — sustained over time. Consistency beats intensity: professional persistence, always paired with something of value, wins more often than a flurry of activity in week one that fades by week three.

Common Misconceptions

MisconceptionReality
"It's just cold calling."Calls matter, but outbound is multi-channel by necessity — customers engage differently and effective SDRs adapt.
"More activity always wins."One well-researched email to the right stakeholder often outperforms dozens of generic ones.
"No response means no interest."Silence usually means busy, evaluating internally, or bad timing — not disinterest. Professional persistence surfaces opportunities that a single attempt would miss.
"The goal is booking meetings."Meetings are a means, not the target. The target is a qualified opportunity that's actually worth the customer's and the AE's time.

Three Questions Behind Every Good Outbound Motion

Why would this organization benefit from talking to Trimble? Who's most likely to care about the problem we solve? What insight or question can I offer that earns the right to keep the conversation going?

Keep these in view and outreach naturally gets more relevant and more consultative — the alternative is optimizing for volume and hoping something lands.

03The Outbound Mindset

Most days start with no queue waiting for you — no demo requests, no inbound inquiries. Every conversation begins with your initiative, which is exactly what makes the role both energizing and hard. Nobody succeeds here off one great email or one exceptional cold call; it's the mindset behind the daily work that actually compounds.

Curiosity Over Pitching

Customers don't want another pitch — they want someone who understands their business. That means listening more than you speak and learning before recommending. Swap "how do I convince them to meet with us?" for "what can I learn about their business that makes this conversation worth having?" Curiosity earns trust; trust is what creates the opportunity in the first place.

Consistency Beats Intensity

One exceptional day followed by a week of inconsistent effort doesn't produce predictable pipeline — daily fundamentals do: researching accounts every morning, completing the outreach you planned, following up when you said you would, keeping Salesforce current, reviewing your own calls. Small actions repeated consistently outperform occasional bursts every time.

Handling Rejection

Not every prospect responds, and not every conversation moves forward — that's the job, not a signal something's wrong with your approach. Often it has nothing to do with you: wrong timing, a budget freeze, a team mid-project, genuine busyness. Swap "they rejected me" for "the timing or circumstances weren't right," and treat every conversation as information that sharpens the next one.

Playing the Long Game

Enterprise and mid-market sales rarely happen fast. A conversation today might lead to a meeting six months out; a meeting this quarter might become an opportunity next year. Invest in the relationship, not just this week's outcome — persistence builds familiarity, familiarity builds credibility, and credibility is what eventually creates the opportunity.

Confidence Without Pressure

Customers respond to reps who are knowledgeable, prepared, and genuinely interested in helping — and disengage fast from anything that feels scripted or pushy. Confidence comes from preparation and product knowledge, not from controlling the conversation. Ask good questions, speak clearly, get comfortable with silence, and let the conversation move naturally. Your job is to invite a conversation, not force one.

Customer-First Prospecting

Every outreach should be able to answer one question honestly:

"Why should this customer spend time talking with me?"

Focus on business outcomes, industry challenges, and a genuinely relevant insight or question — and resist making it about Trimble too early. Customers engage when they feel understood, not marketed to.

Growth Mindset, Ownership, Resilience, Discipline

The strongest SDRs never assume they've mastered the role. A few habits show up consistently among the ones who keep improving:

TraitIn Practice
Growth MindsetWelcomes coaching, reviews their own calls, tries new techniques, learns from teammates
OwnershipBuilds their own account plans and prioritizes proactively instead of waiting to be told what's next
ResilienceAbsorbs missed calls, unanswered emails, and lost opportunities without letting them define the week
DisciplineProtects prospecting time and follows the plan even on low-motivation days

None of these are personality traits you either have or don't — they're habits, built the same way the daily-execution habits in "Consistency Beats Intensity" are built.

Bringing It Together

The strongest Outbound SDRs are curious before they're persuasive, consistent instead of sporadic, patient during long cycles, confident without being aggressive, and customer-focused rather than product-focused. None of that shows up as a single skill you either have or don't — it's a set of daily choices that compound, and it's the foundation everything else in this playbook builds on.

PART II

Understanding Trimble

04Understanding Trimble & the AECO Business

Customers rarely buy software because it has more features than the alternative — they invest because they're trying to solve a business problem, reduce risk, or get ahead of where their operations are headed. You don't need to become a product expert to be effective here. You need to understand Trimble, the industries we serve, and our customers' challenges well enough to create a conversation that's actually relevant to them.

You are not expected to be a product expert. You're expected to understand enough about Trimble's business and the industries we serve to ask thoughtful questions, identify opportunities, and confidently guide customers to the right resources.

Who Is Trimble?

Trimble is a global technology company that connects the physical and digital worlds through software, hardware, and data. For decades, Trimble has helped customers improve productivity, quality, safety, and sustainability by digitizing workflows across the industries that shape the world around us — Architecture, Engineering, Construction, Geospatial, Transportation, Agriculture, Utilities, Government, and Natural Resources. While each industry has unique needs, they all share a common goal: helping people work smarter by connecting information, people, and processes.

Trimble's Purpose

Trimble's purpose is to transform the way the world works. Rather than focusing solely on individual software products, Trimble develops connected technology ecosystems that enable organizations to plan, design, build, and operate more efficiently. Customers rely on Trimble to reduce manual work, improve collaboration, increase visibility, make better decisions, minimize risk, and deliver projects more efficiently.

Every conversation with a prospect should reinforce that Trimble is more than a software vendor — we are a long-term technology partner invested in improving business outcomes.

What Is AECO?

AECO stands for Architecture, Engineering, Construction, and Owner & Operator. These industries are responsible for creating and maintaining the built environment — commercial buildings, residential developments, hospitals, schools, airports, roads and highways, bridges, manufacturing facilities, utilities, and public infrastructure. AECO organizations manage complex projects involving numerous stakeholders, tight schedules, evolving budgets, and significant operational risk. Trimble provides technology that helps these organizations work together more effectively from initial concept through long-term operations.

You don't need to be a technical software engineer, but you must speak the native language of the built environment.

The AECO Landscape

  • A – Architecture: Conceptual 3D models, visual design collaboration, spec writing.
  • E – Engineering: Structural/civil design, clash detection, constructability.
  • C – Construction: General Contractors (GCs), Specialty Subcontractors (MEP, Steel, Concrete), Civil/Heavy Infrastructure.
  • O – Owners & Public Sector: Municipalities, government agencies, capital project leaders.

The Problem: A Fragmented Industry

Construction is a team sport played by a large, shifting cast — owners, architects, engineers, general contractors, specialty subcontractors, field crews, and operations teams, often spread across dozens of vendors and subcontracts on a single project. Historically, those teams have relied on manual processes and disconnected systems, creating silos where information gets lost, data becomes trapped in spreadsheets, and communication breaks down between departments, project phases, and the office and field. The result is familiar across the industry: delays compound, mistakes get repeated, budgets get harder to control, and contractor margins are put under pressure.

A snapshot of the roles orbiting a single project team — each with its own priorities, tools, and blind spots.

The cost of that disconnection isn't small. 90% of construction projects experience cost overruns, with the average project landing 28% over budget. Nearly half — 48% of all rework on a jobsite — traces back to nothing more than poor data and miscommunication.

As projects become larger and more complex, organizations are investing in BIM, estimating, project management, field operations, equipment management, scheduling, business intelligence, and other technologies to close those gaps. This broader shift is often described as digital transformation — not simply buying new software, but changing how work gets done in response to labor shortages, rising material costs, tighter schedules, and margin pressure. Understanding this trend gives you useful context for customer conversations because many of the problems prospects describe ultimately connect back to how information, people, and workflows move across the business.

The Vision: Connected Construction

The industry's response to that fragmentation is a move toward Connected Construction — connecting people, processes, and data across the full project lifecycle rather than treating construction as a rigid series of isolated handoffs. The goal is for information to flow between departments, systems, and project phases so teams can work from shared, current information instead of disconnected versions of the truth. That creates faster feedback loops between the office and field and gives business leaders better visibility into financial and operational performance while the project is still underway — not weeks after it has closed.

The Connected Construction Lifecycle

Understanding where a prospect fits within this lifecycle helps you ask more relevant discovery questions and route them to the appropriate sales team.

Stage What Happens Stakeholders Typical Challenges
Plan Planning, budgeting, feasibility studies, and scheduling Owners, Developers, Project Managers Budget uncertainty, resource planning, project forecasting
Design Architects and engineers create drawings, models, specifications, and construction documentation Architects, Structural Engineers, Civil Engineers, MEP Engineers Coordination across disciplines, design revisions, version control, collaboration
Estimate Contractors evaluate project costs before bidding Estimators, Preconstruction Teams, Operations Leaders Material pricing, labor availability, bid accuracy, time constraints
Build Construction teams execute the work in the field General Contractors, Specialty Contractors, Superintendents, Field Engineers Schedule delays, labor shortages, safety, RFIs, change orders, communication gaps
Operate Owners manage and maintain their assets once construction is complete Facility Managers, Owners, Asset Managers Maintenance planning, asset visibility, compliance, operational efficiency

Trimble Construction One (TC1): Bridging the Gap

This is the gap Trimble exists to close. Rather than information passing through a slow, lossy "game of telephone" between the architect's desk, the office, and the jobsite, Trimble connects all three so everyone works from the same data at the same time. Trimble Construction One (TC1) is the product ecosystem that makes this real — effectively an all-in-one digital operating system for a construction company, pulling data out of isolated spreadsheets and into a single shared cloud environment. If a manager updates a blueprint or a budget in the office Tuesday morning, the field crew sees it on their tablets that same afternoon — no re-entry, no waiting around, and no expensive mistakes built on stale information.

On paper, a project looks like a clean, linear assembly line — design it, estimate it, build it, operate it. In practice it behaves more like a wheel than a line: data doesn't sit quietly inside one phase, it gets handed off dynamically. When an architect changes a 3D model, that change alters material costs, which changes what the crew measures on site, which eventually changes the final asset record an owner operates against. The five pillars below are how TC1 actually organizes that wheel into a product ecosystem — and the lifecycle table after it shows how they map across a project's life.

The "TC1 Wheel" — you'll see this shape again throughout the playbook. It's the same five pillars below, shown as one connected system instead of a product list.

Why Customers Buy Trimble

Customers rarely begin by saying "I need new software." Instead, they describe business problems — "Our estimating takes too long," "Our teams don't communicate well," "We're constantly behind schedule," "Our field crews are using outdated information," "We have too much manual work," "We struggle to track project costs," "Our models don't stay coordinated." These business problems create opportunities for meaningful discovery. As an SDR, your role is to understand the underlying challenge — not immediately recommend a product.

Every customer is different, but the outcomes they're chasing tend to cluster into a handful of themes:

OutcomeWhat It Looks Like
ProductivityLess manual work, more accomplished with the same team
VisibilityLeaders get real access to project, operational, and financial information
CollaborationOffice, field, design, and construction teams actually stay connected
Reduced RiskBetter accuracy, less rework, issues caught earlier in the lifecycle
ProfitabilityMore efficient operations translate into better financial performance
GrowthTechnology that scales with the business instead of becoming a constraint

Key Pain Points by Deal Size

The problems above show up everywhere. This is the more specific version — where Mid-Market and Enterprise firms feel the same pain, and where their situations actually diverge.

Mid-Market $10–49.9M$50M+
Similarity
  • Too many disparate solutions. Trying to solve needs with bolt-ons is ultimately expensive, and frustrating to manage. Both Mid-Market and Enterprise firms are looking to save money and improve efficiency and visibility by connecting different parts of their business into one dataset. Trying to pull data into spreadsheets to get a clear understanding of what's happening is time-consuming and error-prone. They need trustworthy, real-time cost data to manage with.
  • Field and office disconnected. Both Mid-Market and Enterprise firms struggle with inefficient communication between accounting and what's actually happening on the jobsite. Enterprise firms and many Mid-Market firms have construction-focused ERP solutions already, but they aren't cloud-based and/or they have to go to a third party to try to connect field tools from other vendors. It's expensive, and doesn't always work well. Getting help with issues can be frustrating, because each provider says it's someone else's problem.
  • Mid-Market and Enterprise firms need field tools that connect and are easy to use, so that their workers actually adopt them. If people don't or can't use the tools, they're paying for nothing.
  • Growth goals and challenges are prominent in both segments, because the inefficiencies of disconnected data create heavy workloads for both Accounting and PM staff — they can't hire enough people to solve the issues that growth creates.
Differences
  • Many Mid-Market firms use Quickbooks for accounting, which doesn't provide detailed job cost data.
  • Too much time-consuming manual work to see job costs — sometimes they don't know how a job performed until it's already over.
  • Lack of automation impedes growth, because as they add more and bigger jobs, they struggle more to manage without real-time reporting.
  • Larger firms have more lines of business and custom workflows — they need to track many different unique items through User Defined Fields, so they need highly customizable reporting.
  • Have invested but haven't seen the growth or technical improvements they expect.
  • Need better analytics in order to identify where to focus and where to pull back across business divisions.

Business Outcomes Customers Care About

Customers evaluate technology based on the outcomes it helps them achieve: increased productivity, better collaboration, reduced project risk, improved profitability, faster project delivery, greater visibility into project performance, reduced rework, better decision-making, improved field efficiency, more accurate estimating, and higher-quality deliverables. Whenever possible, connect discovery conversations back to business outcomes rather than product features.

The Industries You Might Support

Trimble's Outbound org is organized around five industry segments — Civil, MEP, General Contracting, Structures, and ERP Cross-Sell — each with its own priorities, personas, and buying triggers. Section 7 is the full reference for whichever one you're assigned to; this chapter stays at the company level.

Your Role

You're not expected to have every answer. You're expected to understand the industries you support, recognize the challenges that come up again and again, do enough research to ask a sharp question, and know when to bring in your AE. Think of yourself as the first chapter of the customer's relationship with Trimble — the quality of that first conversation is what earns the right to a second one.

06Differentiation & Positioning

Section 4 covered what Trimble is and who it serves. This is the applied version — how to actually talk about why Trimble, without a feature dump, and how to handle it when a competitor comes up.

The Core Wedge: Connected Data, Not Another Point Solution

Most AECO software competitors win a single pillar — design, PM, or field — and stop there. Trimble Construction One's differentiation is that the pillars share data: an estimate flows into a project budget, field production data flows into billing, and none of it requires someone retyping a spreadsheet at 9pm. When a prospect describes double-entry, reconciliation lag, or "our systems don't talk to each other," that is the wedge — lead with it before you lead with any single product name.

Positioning Pillars

Use conversationally, not as a pitch.

  1. Field-to-office connectivity. Data created in the field (survey, layout, production) or in precon (estimates, takeoffs) flows through to the office (PM, accounting) without manual re-entry. Trimble's most defensible claim, because of pillar 3.
  2. Purpose-built for construction, not adapted from generic software. Workflows map to how AECO firms actually operate (bid → award → build → bill).
  3. Hardware + software integration. Decades of field hardware (Total Stations, GNSS, machine control) tied directly into the software stack — hard for software-only competitors to replicate.
  4. Modular entry, connected ceiling. A prospect can start with a single pillar and expand into an adjacent one later without a rip-and-replace, because the data model is already shared.

Competitors

Competitive Landscape

You will occasionally hear customers mention other platforms, point solutions, or existing systems during discovery. Your job is not to immediately prove why Trimble is better. First, understand what the customer uses today, what role it plays in their workflow, and whether there are gaps or challenges worth exploring.

When a competitor comes up, focus on questions like:

  • What are you using today?
  • What is working well with your current approach?
  • Where, if anywhere, are you still experiencing friction?
  • Are all teams using the same system or process?
  • What prompted you to consider something different?

Competitive landscapes vary significantly by industry and workflow. For current competitor information, positioning, differentiators, and approved competitive guidance, reference the appropriate Industry Playbooks.

The gap they describe is your qualification, not something you need to argue.

07Industry Specialization

Relevance is what makes a cold outreach land. A Civil contractor, an MEP firm, a General Contractor, a Structures shop, and an existing ERP customer all sit inside the same broader construction ecosystem, but their priorities, workflows, and technology needs are genuinely different — which means one message doesn't work for all five. You don't need to be a technical expert in every solution area to specialize well. You need enough knowledge of your assigned industry to personalize outreach, ask sharper discovery questions, recognize a real buying signal, and partner effectively with your AE. The goal isn't to tell customers what their challenges are — it's to ask questions informed enough that they want to answer them.

Civil

Civil organizations design, build, and maintain infrastructure — roads, bridges, airports, rail, utilities, land development — ranging from regional contractors to enterprises running complex, multi-site infrastructure programs. Their work depends on coordination between office teams, field crews, equipment operators, and other stakeholders spread across locations.

What they're wrestling with: productivity (completing projects faster, better equipment utilization, less downtime), project complexity (coordinating across many teams and changing site conditions), accuracy and rework (errors in planning or communication turning into costly delays), and field-to-office collaboration (getting information moving fast enough for good decisions).

PersonaTypically Cares About
Executive Leadership (CEO, President, Owner, VP Operations)Growth, profitability, competitive advantage, operational efficiency
Operations Leaders (Director of Ops, VP Construction)Productivity, standardization, project performance, resource management
Project ManagersSchedule management, communication, coordination, risk reduction
Field Leaders (Superintendents, Foremen)Execution, visibility, equipment performance, productivity
Preconstruction (Estimators, Engineers)Bid accuracy, planning, cost control

Buying triggers to watch for: winning a larger project than usual, expansion into a new market, headcount or equipment growth, visible operational inefficiency, or a stated digital transformation initiative.

Discovery starting points: "How is your team measuring productivity today?" "How connected are your field and office teams?" "What processes require the most manual effort right now?" "How are you preparing your operations to scale?"

MEP (Mechanical, Electrical & Plumbing)

MEP organizations design, estimate, fabricate, install, and maintain the mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems inside buildings and infrastructure projects. Their work requires tight coordination between design teams, estimators, fabrication shops, project teams, field crews, and other trades — often while drawings, schedules, and project requirements continue to change.

What they're wrestling with: coordination (keeping designs accurate across trades and project changes), labor productivity (doing more with limited skilled labor), fabrication efficiency (moving work from design into prefabrication with fewer errors), accuracy and rework (catching clashes and mistakes before they reach the field), and workflow consistency (connecting estimating, detailing, fabrication, and installation).

PersonaTypically Cares About
Executive Leadership (Owner, President, VP Operations)Growth, profitability, labor efficiency, risk reduction, scalability
Operations / Construction LeadersProductivity, standardization, resource planning, project performance
Estimating / Preconstruction LeadersBid accuracy, estimating speed, cost visibility, win rates
BIM / VDC / Detailing LeadersCoordination, model accuracy, constructability, design-to-fabrication workflows
Fabrication LeadersShop productivity, material accuracy, prefabrication, reducing waste
Project / Field LeadersInstallation efficiency, change management, coordination, schedule performance

Buying triggers to watch for: increasing project volume, larger or more complex project wins, expansion of prefabrication capabilities, BIM/VDC investment, skilled labor constraints, opening or expanding a fabrication shop, standardization initiatives, or recurring coordination and rework issues.

Discovery starting points: "How does work move from estimating into detailing, fabrication, and the field today?" "Where do project changes create the most disruption?" "How much of your work are you prefabricating today?" "Where does your team still rely on manual handoffs or duplicate data entry?"

General Contracting

General contractors coordinate the overall delivery of a construction project, bringing together owners, architects, engineers, subcontractors, suppliers, and field teams. Their ability to deliver successfully depends on keeping schedules, costs, documentation, communication, and field execution aligned across a large number of stakeholders.

What they're wrestling with: project visibility (knowing what is happening across projects before issues become larger problems), schedule and cost control (keeping work on time and within budget), subcontractor coordination (managing information and accountability across many external partners), risk management (identifying issues early), and field-to-office collaboration (keeping project information current and accessible to the people making decisions).

PersonaTypically Cares About
Executive Leadership (CEO, President, Owner, COO)Growth, profitability, risk, portfolio performance, predictability
Operations Leaders (VP Construction, Director of Operations)Standardization, project performance, resource utilization, visibility
Project Executives / Project DirectorsPortfolio oversight, risk, schedule, financial performance
Project ManagersCost control, documentation, coordination, change management
Superintendents / Field LeadersSchedule execution, field communication, issue resolution, productivity
Preconstruction / EstimatingBid accuracy, planning, constructability, handoff into operations
VDC / Technology LeadersConnected workflows, adoption, integrations, data consistency

Buying triggers to watch for: rapid growth, larger or more complex projects, expansion into new markets, increasing subcontractor volume, inconsistent processes across projects, a new technology or VDC leader, consolidation of point solutions, or an initiative to improve project visibility and standardization.

Discovery starting points: "How do your teams get visibility into project health today?" "Where do you see the biggest disconnect between the office and field?" "How consistent are your project processes from one team or region to another?" "When a project starts moving off plan, how quickly does leadership know?"

Structures

Structures organizations design, engineer, detail, fabricate, and erect the structural components that make up buildings and infrastructure. Depending on the business, that may include structural steel, concrete, precast, or other engineered systems. Their work depends on precision — information has to move accurately from engineering and detailing into fabrication and ultimately into the field.

What they're wrestling with: design coordination (keeping structural information aligned as projects change), accuracy (ensuring models, drawings, and fabrication information match), production efficiency (moving work through detailing and fabrication without unnecessary delays), material and labor utilization (reducing waste and improving throughput), and rework (preventing errors from carrying downstream into fabrication or erection).

PersonaTypically Cares About
Executive Leadership (Owner, President, General Manager)Growth, profitability, capacity, competitive differentiation
Engineering LeadersDesign accuracy, code compliance, coordination, engineering efficiency
Detailing / BIM LeadersModel quality, constructability, coordination, drawing production
Fabrication ManagersShop throughput, production planning, material utilization, accuracy
Project ManagersSchedule, coordination, changes, project profitability
Operations / Erection LeadersField readiness, sequencing, accuracy, installation efficiency

Buying triggers to watch for: increased project volume, larger or more complex project wins, fabrication capacity constraints, shop expansion, investments in automation, hiring or labor challenges, increasing BIM requirements, modernization initiatives, or recurring errors between design, fabrication, and erection.

Discovery starting points: "How does information move from design and detailing into fabrication today?" "Where do changes tend to create the most rework?" "What tends to limit your fabrication capacity?" "How connected are your engineering, detailing, fabrication, and field teams?"

ERP Cross-Sell

ERP Cross-Sell is different from the other motions because these are existing Trimble customers. The goal is not to introduce Trimble from scratch — it is to understand the customer's current environment and identify where an existing relationship could expand to solve additional business problems.

These organizations may already use Trimble within accounting, operations, project management, estimating, field workflows, or another part of the business. Your starting point should always be what they already own, how they use it, and what the broader business is trying to accomplish.

What they're wrestling with: disconnected systems (information living across multiple platforms or manual processes), operational visibility (difficulty seeing financial and project performance together), scalability (processes that worked at a smaller size becoming harder to manage), workflow efficiency (duplicate entry and manual handoffs), and business change (growth, acquisitions, new markets, or new capabilities creating new requirements).

PersonaTypically Cares About
Executive Leadership (CEO, President, Owner, COO)Growth, profitability, visibility, scalability, business performance
Finance Leadership (CFO, Controller)Financial accuracy, reporting, forecasting, controls, cash flow
Operations LeadersProcess consistency, productivity, resource management, operational visibility
IT / Technology LeadersIntegrations, data governance, system consolidation, security, adoption
Project / Construction LeadersProject performance, field-to-office workflows, cost visibility
Department LeadersImproving the specific workflows, processes, or outcomes their teams own

Buying triggers to watch for: business growth, acquisitions, expansion into new markets, new business units or capabilities, leadership changes, disconnected systems, manual processes becoming difficult to scale, a push for greater business visibility, technology consolidation, or an existing customer expressing challenges outside the workflow Trimble currently supports.

Discovery starting points: "What has changed in the business since you originally implemented Trimble?" "Where are teams still working outside your current Trimble environment?" "Are there workflows that still require information to be entered or reconciled manually?" "As the business grows, where are you finding your current processes harder to scale?"

Because this is an existing customer relationship, coordinate with the account owner and relevant internal teams before outreach. Understand what the customer already owns, what conversations are already underway, and where there may be an appropriate expansion opportunity. The mindset is not "What else can we sell them?" It is "Where could we create more value for a customer we already serve?"

Building Your Industry Knowledge

Specialization isn't a one-time onboarding task — it builds through customer conversations, AE feedback, Gong call reviews, and just paying attention to what comes up repeatedly. Every conversation is a chance to learn something that makes the next one better. For formal learning and verification, take advantage of the product and industry certification courses available in Trimble Learn. As deeper industry-specific playbooks get built out (target profiles, messaging by persona, objection handling, customer stories), they'll extend this chapter rather than replace it.

08Trimble Products & Solutions

Trimble's AECO portfolio runs well past 100 products across North America — memorizing it isn't realistic, and it isn't the job. Your job is understanding the business problems customers are trying to solve, the outcomes they want, which solution area might actually help, and when to bring in an AE or subject-matter expert. Nobody wakes up wanting a new construction software platform; they wake up wanting better visibility, less rework, or a way to manage growth without things falling apart. Start there.

Your Primary Resource

The Connected Consultant Solutions Catalog is the reference for solution areas, product families, capabilities, and the customer outcomes each one supports — use it when prepping for account conversations rather than trying to hold the full portfolio in your head. (Confirm the current catalog link with enablement if you don't have it yet.)

Solution Families

Six broad families cover most of the portfolio. Each maps to a recognizable set of customer problems — use these as conversation starters, not a script.

FamilyCustomer ProblemsSample Conversation Starter
Construction Management & CollaborationDisconnected teams, limited project visibility, manual processes"How are your teams sharing project information between office and field today?"
Design & EngineeringDesign coordination, accuracy, connecting design decisions to construction outcomes"What challenges come up when a project moves from design into construction?"
Field & Construction ExecutionLimited real-time info in the field, workflow inefficiency, communication gaps"What processes create the most friction for your field teams?"
Survey, Geospatial & DataCapturing accurate field data, connecting physical environments to digital information"How important is real-time visibility into field conditions for your operations?"
Equipment & ProductivityEquipment utilization, downtime, operational cost"How are you currently measuring equipment productivity?"

Solution Positioning: Start With the Problem

This is the one habit worth building above all others. Skip "Trimble has a solution that does X." Instead: "Many organizations like yours are looking for ways to improve X — I'm curious how your team approaches that today." The conversation should always open on the customer's situation, not Trimble's catalog.

There's a useful distinction underneath this: product knowledge answers "what does this technology do," while solution knowledge answers "why does this matter to this specific customer." Prioritize the second. That means holding onto the problem, the business impact, who's affected, and the outcome they want — more than any feature list.

Where This Goes Wrong

MistakeBetter
Leading with features the customer doesn't yet have context forConnect the capability to the outcome first
Assuming every company shares the same prioritiesAsk, then listen
Trying to introduce the whole portfolio at onceStay focused on the one challenge that's actually on the table
Overpromising on capabilities outside your knowledgeCreate interest, then bring in the right expert

Handing Off to Your AE

You're not expected to independently nail the perfect solution fit — that's a shared job. Your responsibility is spotting the challenge, creating a real conversation, and capturing enough context that the AE isn't starting from zero: customer goals, current challenges, existing processes, key stakeholders, and the business outcome that matters most to them. Strong discovery is what makes a handoff worth having. (Sections 14 and 22 will go into the partnership and handoff expectations with your AEs)

PART III

Territory & Account Planning

09Territory Ownership

Great Outbound SDRs don't treat their territory as a list of accounts to work through — they treat it as a business they're responsible for growing. That's a shift from a task-based question ("what accounts do I need to contact today?") to a strategic one ("where are the best opportunities to create value for customers and build pipeline for Trimble?"). Strong SDRs don't wait for opportunity to appear. They actively create it.

What Territory Ownership Means

Owning a territory means becoming the expert on your assigned market: which companies are in it, which align with Trimble's ICP, which represent the biggest opportunity, what challenges those organizations likely face, who the key stakeholders are, and what events might create urgency. None of this is static — companies grow, leadership changes, projects start, priorities shift. The job includes continuously updating your read on the territory, not just building it once.

Balancing Two Time Horizons

A territory strategist holds two things at once: short-term pipeline creation (engaging active prospects, following up on buying signals, booking discovery calls) and long-term market development (building relationships with strategic accounts and future buyers that won't pay off this quarter). Favoring only one leaves either your pipeline or your future pipeline thin.

Understanding the Landscape You Own

Before executing outreach, get oriented on three things.

  • Market composition — how many target accounts you have, which industry segments and company sizes they span, and where Trimble already has a presence.
  • Account landscape — which accounts are strategic, which are growing.
  • Industry trends — market shifts, technology adoption patterns, and industry events that give you a relevant reason to reach out.

Building a Territory Plan

Without a plan, SDRs default to reacting instead of strategically creating pipeline. A plan should answer who you're targeting and why, who the key contacts are, what challenges might create an opening, how you'll engage, and how you'll measure progress. The mechanics of account tiering and prioritization live in Section 10; the mechanics of building a plan for a specific strategic account live in Section 11. This chapter is about the territory-level view that sits above both.

Coverage vs. Depth

A recurring tension: more accounts contacted, or deeper engagement with fewer? The honest answer is both, applied selectively — broad coverage is how you find opportunity, and deep engagement is what turns a promising account into a qualified one. Enterprise accounts in particular need more research, more stakeholders, and more persistence than a quick email allows. Strategic accounts should get strategic effort; not every account deserves the same investment.

Keeping the Territory Current

Review your territory on a regular cadence, not just when something breaks — new accounts appear, markets shift, and engagement levels change. Protect real time for research and planning so your day doesn't become entirely reactive. Every interaction generates intelligence worth capturing: a customer priority, an organizational change, a technology insight. And periodically ask what's actually converting, which messages are landing, and where the patterns are — territory strategy should update based on what you're learning, not stay fixed from the plan you wrote in January.

The difference shows up in the question you ask yourself each morning. A reactive SDR asks "who should I call next?" A territory owner asks "which conversation will create the greatest value for this customer and for Trimble?"

The Golden Rule of Territory

Unless you're specifically told otherwise, you're only allowed to reach out to accounts that are in your AE's name — this applies to any Account record that already exists in Salesforce DX.

For a company that isn't in DX yet, you can call it if you have good reason to believe it's actually in your territory and GAR range — don't call blind on a hope. If you get on the phone and realize partway through that the company is outside your territory, don't just drop it: do your best to still book the meeting and hand it to the appropriate AE. You'll get credit for that.

If you book an SAO on an account that already exists in DX but isn't in your AE's name, that credit can be withheld. Confirm ownership before you invest real time in an account, not after you've booked the meeting.

10Target Accounts & Ideal Customer Profile (ICP)

More activity doesn't automatically create more pipeline — the quality of the accounts you pursue shapes the quality of the opportunities you create. A strategic SDR doesn't ask how many accounts they can contact today; they ask which accounts have the greatest potential to actually benefit from a conversation with Trimble. Account selection is where good outbound strategy starts.

Ideal Client Profile (ICP) answers one question: is this the type of company, and the type of person, Trimble may actually be able to help? It's a lens for fit — not a pass/fail gate, and not where intent or buying signal get evaluated (Section 9 owns that). A strong match earns priority and a sharper conversation; a weak one isn't an automatic disqualify. Treat everything below as signals worth investigating, not conclusions to jump to before you've actually talked to the prospect.

Firmographic Fit

ICP vs. Buyer Persona

These answer two different questions, and conflating them is a common early mistake.

Ideal Customer ProfileBuyer Persona
Answers"Which companies should we target?""Who within that company should we engage?"
