The right account with the wrong contact stalls. The right contact at the wrong account caps your upside. You need both to line up.

What Makes an Account a Fit

What Makes an Account a Fit When evaluating a potential target, weigh industry alignment (does it sit in Civil, MEP, GC, Structures, or Architecture, where Trimble has real expertise?), company size and complexity (does the scale of the operation make a technology investment meaningful?), operational complexity (multiple teams, multiple sites, and field-office coordination usually mean more room for Trimble to help), and growth potential (expanding teams, new markets, and bigger projects tend to create new technology needs).

Note: It is crucial to distinguish between Account Fit and Persona Fit. Your ICP criteria tells you whether the organization is a likely fit, but it does not dictate whether the specific person you are engaging is the ultimate economic buyer. They may be an end user, a technical evaluator, or a researcher. Do not write off a strong account fit just because the initial contact isn’t the senior persona you expected. Instead, use the conversation to understand their internal dynamics and use their context to multi-thread to the right stakeholders.

Buying Signals & Trigger Events

Great SDRs don't wait for a customer to announce they're buying — they watch for signals that a relevant need or window of opportunity exists.

SignalWhy It Matters
Growth (hiring, new locations, expansion, rising project volume)Growth creates operational strain that technology often has to catch up to
Leadership changes (new executives, ops or technology leaders)New leaders tend to evaluate existing processes and look for improvement
New projects or contractsNew work often demands better workflows and more efficiency than the current setup provides
Digital transformation initiativesAn organization already investing in improvement is more open to a relevant conversation
Mergers, acquisitions, or new fundingStructural change tends to force process and technology consolidation
Visible operational challenges (scaling pain, labor constraints, inefficiency)Pain creates urgency — and a reason for the conversation to matter now

Account Tiering

Not every account deserves the same investment. A simple three-tier structure keeps that decision consistent:

TierCharacteristicsApproach
Tier 1 — StrategicStrong ICP fit, enterprise potential, real executive engagement possibleHighly personalized, multi-threaded, long-term relationship investment
Tier 2 — High PotentialGood ICP fit, clear business need, room to growPersonalized outreach, targeted messaging, consistent cadence
Tier 3 — DevelopmentFits the profile but under-researched or early-stageEfficient outreach, prioritized by research, monitored for signals

How to Prioritize Within a Tier

Five factors, applied consistently, keep prioritization from becoming a gut call:

  • fit - ICP alignment
  • pain - evidence of a challenge Trimble can address
  • timing - a reason this account might be open now
  • access - can you actually reach the relevant stakeholders; and
  • potential - does this represent real business value if it converts

A small share of accounts in any territory will score well across all five — that's where the majority of your strategic effort should go. The goal isn't maximum coverage; it's maximum impact.

Before You Reach Out

Account selection sets the direction; research is what makes the first message land. Section 12 is the full playbook for that — don't skip it in favor of a quick LinkedIn glance.

11Building Account Plans

More calls, emails, and LinkedIn messages don't automatically create better results — the highest-performing SDRs do the thinking before the first outreach, not after. That's the real shift in this role: from find contacts → send messages → schedule meetings to understand the business → identify opportunities → engage stakeholders → create conversations → build pipeline. An account plan is what makes that shift concrete — a strategic view of a target account that helps you and your AE agree on why it matters, who's involved, and how you'll engage over time.

This matters more in Mid-Market and Enterprise selling specifically because these deals rarely move through one conversation with one person. A plan is what turns "I found a contact" into "I understand the organization and have a strategy for the right people."

What's In a Plan

Account overview, organizational structure, stakeholder map, business priorities, technology landscape, relevant trigger events, an engagement strategy, and an AE partnership plan. Not every account needs all of this in full depth — Tier 1 accounts (Section 10) warrant the complete version; Tier 3 accounts warrant a lighter pass.

Mapping the Account Hierarchy

Large organizations rarely have one entry point. A single business unit can have its own priorities, its own technology needs, and its own decision-makers — so before reaching out, get a rough picture of the company's structure: business units, regional teams, operating groups, and who owns strategic decisions versus operational execution. A simple version might look like: executive leadership at the top, business leadership below it (VP Operations, VP Construction, VP Technology, VP Engineering), and functional users below that (PMs, superintendents, estimators, field teams). The point isn't a perfect org chart — it's knowing where in that structure your conversation is most likely to be relevant.

Buying Roles: Who's Who in the Decision

Not every contact plays the same role. Section 2 already covers the basic case for multi-threading; here's the taxonomy for identifying who's who once you're inside an account.

RoleCares AboutHow to Spot Them
Economic BuyerStrategic impact, ROI, business priorities — owns the investment decision"Who owns this initiative?" "Who would approve the investment?"
ChampionSolving the problem, improving the process, building internal alignment"Who's most affected by this challenge?" "Who's motivated to fix it?"
InfluencerHas input but doesn't own the decision — often a technical or department lead"Who uses this process today?" "Who'd be involved in implementation?"

Installed Technology & the Competitive Landscape

Customers rarely evaluate technology in a vacuum — they already have platforms, workflows, and preferences that shape how a new conversation lands. Understand what they're currently running, who else they might be evaluating or already using, and where the current setup is visibly limiting them (manual work, duplicate processes, no integration). Good discovery questions here: "What systems are currently part of this workflow?" "How well do your tools work together today?" "What would you improve about your current process?"

Trigger Events, Applied

Section 10 covers the full taxonomy of buying signals and trigger events. Once you've spotted one for a specific account, the job here is connecting it to your plan: what does this trigger imply about who's newly relevant, what conversation it opens, and how soon you should act on it before the window closes.

Multi-Threading in Practice

Start with one entry point — a relevant challenge and an initial contact. Expand deliberately from there to other leaders, users, and technical stakeholders. Then connect the conversations: look for where an operations leader's efficiency concern, a project leader's visibility concern, a technology leader's integration concern, and an executive's growth concern actually point at the same underlying opportunity. That alignment across roles is usually what turns a single relationship into a real opportunity.

Partnering With Your AE: The 30/60/90

A joint SDR/AE strategy session should cover why this account, why now, who owns which relationship, what the messaging angle is, and how engagement will actually happen. For a strategic account, a 30/60/90 structure keeps that strategy on track:

WindowGoalActions
Days 1–30Understand and mapComplete account research, build the stakeholder map, form an opportunity hypothesis, align with your AE, begin outreach
Days 31–60Engage and learnMulti-thread outreach, run real discovery conversations, expand relationships, adjust messaging based on what you're hearing
Days 61–90Build the opportunityRealign with your AE, prioritize the strongest threads, document what you've learned, define the next-step strategy

Before You Engage a Strategic Account, Confirm

You understand the company (industry, business model, priorities, growth signals), the people (economic buyer, champion, influencers, users), the opportunity (business challenges, technology landscape, trigger events, potential value), and you have an actual engagement strategy (messaging, channels, timeline, AE alignment). If any of those four are blank, the plan isn't ready yet — more research beats a rushed first touch.

12Account Research

Research is the difference between "I wanted to introduce Trimble and see if you're interested in learning more" and "I noticed your organization is expanding its infrastructure project portfolio — many companies experiencing similar growth are looking for ways to improve visibility across teams. I was curious how your team is approaching that today." Same intent, completely different odds of a reply. The gap is insight, and insight comes from research done with a purpose, not research done for its own sake.

Quality Over Quantity

The goal isn't to gather everything knowable about an account — it's to find what actually improves the conversation. Before you spend time on a data point, ask: will this help me have a better conversation? If the honest answer is no, it's probably not worth the time, no matter how interesting it is.

What to Look For

AreaWhat to Look For
Company basicsSize, industry focus, locations, services, project types, growth trajectory
LeadershipNew executives, ops or technology leaders, recent promotions — new leaders often evaluate existing processes
Business initiativesExpansion plans, strategic priorities, operational improvement programs, tech investments
Company newsPress releases, announcements, partnerships, awards, acquisitions — recent events are natural conversation hooks
Construction projectsRecent awards, large developments, geographic expansion — among the strongest AECO-specific buying signals
Technology stackCurrent platforms, tech partnerships, signs of disconnected workflows or modernization efforts
Hiring trendsMore PMs may signal growth; more field roles may signal project volume; tech roles may signal digital transformation
Financial signalsRevenue growth, new investment, market performance — for private companies, infer from hiring and project activity instead

Where to Look

ZoomInfo is your fastest path to company data, org structure, and contact information — use it to identify target contacts and build account lists, not as a substitute for judgment. LinkedIn surfaces leadership changes, company updates, and what a specific leader is actually talking about, which is often the most personalized detail you'll find. Company websites (about, leadership, project portfolio, and news pages specifically) show you how the company wants to be seen, which tells you their priorities. Industry publications keep you fluent in the broader trends your customers are already discussing.

Building a Research Brief

Before engaging a strategic account, capture a short brief: the account overview (name, industry, location, size, focus), why this account (ICP fit, opportunity, relevant challenges), recent insights (news, projects, leadership changes), the personas worth targeting and why they'd care, and an outreach hypothesis stated as a single sentence: "I believe this organization may be interested in discussing ______ because ______." For example: "I believe this organization may be interested in discussing improving project visibility because they're expanding operations across multiple locations."

Three Questions Before You Reach Out

  • 1. Why them — why is this company worth engaging?
  • 2. Why now — what signal suggests the timing is right?
  • 3. Why Trimble — what business challenge might we actually help with? If you can't answer all three, that's a sign to research more before sending anything.

Research Only Helps If It Shows Up in the Message

Weak personalization states a fact: "I saw your company has been around for 50 years." Strong personalization connects the fact to a likely priority: "I noticed your team recently expanded into additional markets — organizations experiencing similar growth often look for ways to improve consistency and visibility across operations." The goal isn't proving you did the research. It's showing why it matters to them.

Where Research Goes Wrong

MistakeBetter
Researching too much before ever reaching outFind one or two insights that actually change your message, then act
Researching too little, sending generic outreachAt minimum, answer the Why Them / Why Now / Why Trimble test above
Citing facts with no connection to a priorityTranslate the fact into what it implies about their business
Treating research as a one-time stepCompanies change constantly — keep learning through the relationship, not just before the first touch

Research becomes more valuable shared than kept to yourself — loop your AE in on account strategy, stakeholder mapping, and anything you've learned that shapes the opportunity hypothesis. It sharpens the whole motion, not just your next email.

PART IV

Prospecting Excellence

13Building an Outbound Strategy

Outbound success doesn't come from sending more emails or making more calls — it comes from strategy applied consistently. Every account is a unique situation: a different organization, different people, different challenges, and a different reason a conversation would actually be worth having. The goal was never to contact people. It's to create relationships that lead somewhere.

From Contacts to Accounts

Traditional prospecting thinks in contacts: find someone, send an email, make a call. Strategic outbound thinks in accounts: understand the business, identify the opportunity, engage the right stakeholders. That shift matters most for Enterprise and Mid-Market accounts, where a decision rarely rests with one person and relationship-building takes real time.

Account-Based Prospecting

This is the discipline of prioritizing specific accounts and building a deliberate engagement strategy around each one, instead of reaching broadly at anyone who might be interested. In practice it's four steps: identify the opportunity (why this account, why now, why Trimble — the same test from Section 12, applied at the strategy level), define a hypothesis for why they might care, identify who actually experiences the problem versus who owns the budget versus who'd benefit from a fix, and build the engagement plan — messaging, channels, timing, and how your AE fits in. None of this works as a one-time exercise; it's a loop that tightens as discovery confirms or corrects your hypothesis.

Persona Mapping

Different roles inside the same account care about different outcomes, which means your messaging can't be one-size-fits-all. Section 16 has the full persona-by-persona messaging guidance — the short version is that executives tend to care about growth and strategic positioning, operations leaders about efficiency and standardization, project leaders about schedule and coordination, and technical users about workflow and integration. Knowing which persona you're talking to should shape the conversation before you ever open your mouth.

Contact Prioritization

This is a different axis from the account tiering in Section 10 — that's about which accounts deserve the most investment; this is about which contacts within an account deserve the most effort. Weigh influence (how much impact does this person have on the decision), relevance (do they actually experience the problem you're addressing), access (can you realistically build a relationship with them), and timing (is there a reason they'd be open to this now).

Contact TierExamplesApproach
Tier 1Executives, business owners, decision-makers, strategic influencersHighly personalized, account-specific, multi-channel
Tier 2Operations leaders, project leaders, department headsPersona-based messaging, problem-focused outreach
Tier 3Individual contributors, users, broader team membersRelationship building, learning-focused conversations

Personalization and Sequencing

Not every touch needs the same depth of personalization, and very few opportunities come from a single interaction. Section 16 covers the personalization levels (account, persona, and trigger-based) and Section 18 covers how to sequence touches across channels — both are core to executing the strategy this chapter sets up.

Where Outbound Strategy Breaks Down

MistakeBetter
Contacting only one person at the accountBuild relationships across the org (Section 11 has the full multi-threading approach)
Sending generic messagingConnect outreach to a specific business challenge
Prioritizing activity over strategyVolume without a strategy behind it rarely converts
Giving up after one or two touchesMost real opportunities need multiple interactions to surface

Outbound success was never about reaching the most people — it's about creating the right conversation with the right customer at the right time. Strategy is what turns activity into opportunity.

14SDR & AE Partnership

An SDR can't create meaningful pipeline alone, and an AE can't effectively work an account without the intelligence and early relationship-building an SDR provides. The relationship works best under shared ownership — shared accounts, shared strategy, shared accountability — rather than a relay-race handoff where "the SDR books the meeting and the AE takes over." That framing creates gaps. The stronger version: the SDR and AE work together to create, develop, and advance opportunities, starting well before any meeting gets booked, during account planning itself (Section 11).

This section will give you a high level overview of the partnership expectations for yourself and your AE. For more detailed information on roles and responsibilities, rules of engagement, tier definitions, and more - please see the SDR & AE Partnership Playbook.

Who Owns What

The SDR owns territory intelligence (target accounts, industry trends, customer signals), account engagement (outreach strategy, prospect conversations, stakeholder relationships), pipeline creation (new conversations, qualified opportunities), and surfacing customer insight back to the team. The AE owns account strategy (industry expertise, opportunity strategy), customer engagement once a conversation is underway (discovery, solution alignment), opportunity progression (evaluation, business case, next steps), and coaching the SDR on messaging and prospecting. Both jointly own territory success, account prioritization, pipeline creation, and the customer's overall experience — those aren't things either role delivers alone.

Planning the Territory Together

A territory isn't just a list of accounts — it's a shared business opportunity, and SDR/AE alignment on it should cover the territory overview (segments, geography, market opportunity), account priorities (what needs immediate focus vs. nurturing vs. more research), coverage strategy (who owns engaging which accounts and personas), and shared success measures (pipeline goals, activity expectations, conversion targets). Section 9 covers how an SDR thinks about territory solo; this is the version done jointly with your AE.

Weekly Planning

Without a regular cadence, SDR and AE work drifts apart even with the best intentions. A weekly planning conversation should cover: territory review (priority accounts, new signals, any strategy shifts), prospecting focus (who's being targeted, which personas, what messaging), pipeline creation (new meetings, opportunities identified), blockers (difficult accounts, competitive intel, resources needed), and clear next actions with owners attached. Fifteen minutes of real alignment here saves hours of working at cross-purposes later.

Selecting Accounts Together

Section 10 already covers the account-selection criteria (fit, pain, timing, access, potential) in full — use that same framework here rather than building a separate one. What's different in this context is that the decision should be made jointly: an SDR's read on ICP fit and buying signals paired with an AE's read on strategic value and long-term relationship potential produces a sharper prioritization than either working alone.

Joint Prospecting

Some of the strongest engagement comes from SDR and AE working an account together rather than in sequence. In executive outreach, the SDR identifies the target and handles research and outreach execution while the AE contributes industry credibility and an executive-level perspective to the messaging. In a strategic account campaign, the SDR maps stakeholders and builds the engagement plan while the AE shapes account strategy and supports customer conversations as they start. Around events, the SDR identifies targets and coordinates outreach beforehand, both build relationships during, and both follow up after — nobody's chasing a lead alone that the other already has context on.

Feedback Runs Both Ways

SDRs are positioned to notice prospect reactions, market signals, and which messaging is actually landing — that's valuable input for the AE and for refining outreach. AEs are positioned to notice meeting quality, discovery outcomes, and qualification gaps — equally valuable input back to the SDR. Good feedback is specific and actionable, not a verdict. "The meeting wasn't good" teaches nothing; "the prospect was interested, but we needed more detail on business impact before advancing" gives the SDR something to actually adjust.

Pipeline Reviews Are Strategy Sessions, Not Status Checks

An SDR should come ready to discuss which accounts are being targeted, what's been created, and where the friction is. An AE should come ready to share what's working in the opportunities that have advanced and what context would help going forward. The real questions worth asking together: are we engaging the right accounts and the right personas, is there a genuine business challenge and urgency behind what's in the pipeline, and what should change about where we're focusing next.

Shared Accountability, In Practice

Neither "the AE owns the opportunity now" nor "the SDR just needs to create more meetings" reflects how this actually works well. The better question, asked by both sides: what can we do together to create a better outcome here? Partnerships that operate this way tend to track three things together — activity (accounts engaged, conversations created), quality (meeting quality, conversion, pipeline contribution), and collaboration itself (planning consistency, feedback exchange, strategy alignment).

Rules of Engagement With AEs

The problem this exists to avoid: SDRs sending an AE a hundred DX links asking "can I reach out to this person?" Assuming the account is already in your territory (Section 9), a simple test decides whether you need to ask first:

  • No open opportunity on the account? Call anyone. If you notice your AE reached out recently, or has a future task logged against a record on that account, it's your call whether to give them a heads-up — you don't have to ask permission.
  • Open opportunity on the account? Ask the AE first. The COO might be mid-cycle on ProjectSight, but that doesn't mean the Controller isn't a legitimate ERP conversation — the AE just needs to be looped in before you start it.
  • Opportunity Closed Won in the last 6 months? Ask the AE first. There are plenty of good reasons not to pitch a new product onto an account that just bought something — let the AE make that call.

Rules of Engagement With Other SDRs

If an Inbound SDR is actively working Prospect A at a company, an Outbound SDR is free to work Prospect B at that same company — whoever books the meeting first gets the SAO credit. What you don't do is reach out to a prospect a colleague is already actively working; check their Gong record before you start a sequence to make sure you're not stepping on an active thread.

Who Owns the Outreach

This is a team game, but ownership does shift at a predictable point. Before the Intro Call, it's the SDR's: calendar invitations, reschedules, pre-meeting follow-up, sending the Google Meet link and agenda. After the Intro Call, if the opportunity moves to Discovery stage, the AE owns any and all follow-up outreach. If it doesn't SQO, it goes back to being a team effort — SDR and AE both work to salvage it, and the SDR shouldn't be shy about taking the reins if that's what moves it forward.

Where Partnerships Break Down

ProblemFix
Teams operating independently with little communicationA consistent planning rhythm, not just ad hoc syncs
SDR and AE defining success differentlyExplicitly agree on roles, goals, and process up front
Feedback rarely happens, so mistakes repeatBuild in a regular, specific feedback exchange
Meetings become the goal instead of the outcomeKeep the focus on conversation quality, not volume

Neither role works for the other. They're partners responsible together for customer value and pipeline — and the strongest ones plan, target, prospect, and improve together rather than in sequence.

15Outbound Messaging

Message quality determines whether a prospect sees your outreach as valuable or as noise. Most sales messages get ignored because they're focused on the seller — what we offer, what we do, why we're different. Effective outbound messaging starts somewhere else entirely: the customer's business, their challenges, and the outcome they're after. The goal was never to sell a product in an email. It's to create enough relevance and curiosity for a real conversation.

Three Questions Every Message Should Answer

  • Why you — why are you reaching out to this specific person?
  • Why this company — why does this organization make sense as a prospect?
  • Why now — what makes this moment relevant?
(This is the same test as the Why Them / Why Now / Why Trimble framework in Section 12, just applied to the message itself rather than the account decision.) A strong message connects customer context, business challenge, and potential value into an actual invitation to talk:

"I noticed your team has been expanding its project portfolio across multiple locations. Organizations experiencing similar growth often look for ways to improve visibility and consistency across operations. I was curious how your team is approaching that today."

Value Over Features

Section 8 already makes the case for leading with outcomes instead of capabilities — this is that principle applied to a single message. Compare feature-based ("Trimble offers software that helps manage construction workflows") to value-based ("Many construction organizations are looking for ways to improve visibility across teams and reduce the friction created by disconnected workflows. I was curious how your organization is approaching that today"). The second one gives the reader something to react to.

A simple formula gets you there: state an observation ("I noticed your company recently expanded into additional markets"), connect it to likely business impact ("organizations growing quickly often face challenges maintaining consistency across teams"), and close with a conversation starter ("how is your team approaching that today?").

Personalization Levels

Not every touch needs the same depth of research behind it — match the effort to the level of personalization you're aiming for.

LevelBased OnExample
AccountCompany info — recent projects, growth, industry focus"I saw your team recently expanded operations into the Southeast."
PersonaRole responsibilities and priorities"Many operations leaders are focused on improving visibility and consistency across projects."
TriggerTiming signals — new leadership, new projects, announcements (see Section 10's full signal list)Reference the specific event directly, then connect it to a likely priority

Good personalization proves you understand why something matters to them — not just that you did research. Avoid stacking irrelevant details just to demonstrate effort; one well-chosen fact beats three generic ones.

Messaging by Persona

PersonaPrioritiesMessage Focus
ExecutiveGrowth, profitability, strategic advantageBusiness outcomes, scalability, competitive position — "Many organizations are looking for ways to improve operational visibility as they scale."
OperationsProductivity, efficiency, standardizationWorkflow improvement, reduced friction — "Many operations teams are evaluating ways to reduce friction between teams and improve execution."
Project ManagementSchedule, coordination, risk reductionCollaboration, visibility, fewer delays — "Teams managing complex projects often look for ways to improve communication and reduce delays."
TechnicalSystems, integration, adoptionTechnology alignment, process improvement, user experience

Email Frameworks

Problem → Insight → Question is the simplest structure for creating curiosity: name a common challenge, share an observation about this account, invite conversation. Trigger-based outreach works when you have a specific reason to engage: reference the trigger, explain why it matters, invite the conversation. Executive outreach should skip product details and technical language entirely and stay at the level of growth, strategy, and efficiency.

Across all three: keep it more "you" than "we," keep it short enough to read in ten seconds, and make the ask a conversation, not a demo request. "Would it be worth comparing notes?" earns more replies than "can I show you a demo?" this early.

Call Structure

A cold call isn't meant to close anything — it's meant to create engagement.

    Structure: introduce yourself and ask permission ("this is an unexpected call, do you have 30 seconds for why I'm reaching out?"), connect to relevance (why you're calling this account specifically), ask a discovery question that invites real dialogue, listen for challenges and priorities, and if there's alignment, propose a concrete next step.

Voicemail Structure

A voicemail's job isn't to deliver your full message — it's to create recognition and a reason to call back. Introduction, reason for calling, one line of value, and a call to action ("I'll send a quick email as well"). Keep it under 20 seconds.

LinkedIn Messaging

LinkedIn outreach should read like relationship-building, not a sales email with a different header. A connection request stays simple and low-pressure; the follow-up after connecting references what you do generally and asks a genuine question about their priorities. Engage with their posts before you ask for anything — familiarity built passively makes the first direct message land better.

Where Messaging Goes Wrong

MistakeBetter
Leading with Trimble before the customer has a reason to careStart with their challenge
Cramming in too much informationCreate just enough interest for a conversation
Generic personalization (a company name isn't relevance)Connect the detail to actual business impact
Asking for too much too soon (a demo request feels premature)Earn the conversation first

Before sending anything, a quick check: why should this person care, why am I contacting them specifically, what business challenge am I connecting to, is the message easy to follow, and is the ask simple? If any of those are shaky, it's worth another pass before you hit send.

16Qualification in Outbound

Outbound prospects didn't raise their hand — which means your first job isn't to qualify interest, it's to create it. Section 2 already covers how outbound differs from inbound at the motion level; the difference that matters here is narrower: inbound discovery usually starts from an existing challenge the prospect already recognizes, while outbound discovery often has to first establish whether a challenge exists worth talking about at all. The goal isn't to sell. It's to uncover.

Earning the Conversation

Prospects don't take a meeting because an SDR wants time on their calendar — they take it because they believe the conversation might be worth something. Three things earn that: relevance (why does this topic matter to this company specifically), curiosity (giving them a genuine reason to think, not just react), and value (making it worthwhile even if nothing comes of it today). Approach every call with "I believe there may be an opportunity to improve something, and I want to understand how you're handling it today" rather than "I already know what your problem is."

Questions That Actually Open Up a Conversation

Keep questions open-ended and business-focused rather than yes/no. Understand the current state ("How is your team managing this today?" "What's working well?"), surface the challenge ("Where do you see the biggest opportunity for improvement?" "Where does your team experience friction?"), get to impact ("How does that affect your team?" "What happens when that issue comes up?"), and check priority ("Is this something your team is actively focused on right now?").

Business Pain, By Type

Pain is the gap between where the customer is and where they want to be — and it shows up in a few recognizable flavors: operational (inefficient workflows, manual processes, poor visibility), financial (rising costs, shrinking margins, lost productivity), strategic (trouble scaling, competitive pressure, unmet digital transformation goals), and people (labor shortages, training gaps, growth outpacing the team). Naming which type you're hearing helps you connect it to the right kind of business impact later in the conversation.

Qualifying Without Checking Boxes

Outbound qualification isn't a checklist — it's confirming there's a real opportunity worth an AE's time. Four things to establish: need (is there a challenge Trimble might help with), impact (does it actually affect the business), priority (is it important enough to act on), and timing (is there a reason to evaluate change now). You're identifying the challenge, the current process, the desired improvement, the relevant stakeholders, and the level of interest — you're not fully diagnosing their environment, positioning every product detail, or doing the AE's discovery for them. You create the opportunity. The AE deepens it.

Handing Off Without Making Them Start Over

The prospect should feel like the next conversation builds on this one, not that they're repeating themselves. Before transitioning to an AE, capture customer context (company, industry, situation), the business challenge and why it matters, the current state and tools in use, the desired outcome, who was involved in the conversation, and why now matters.

The difference between a handoff that works and one that doesn't is entirely about specificity:

Weak: "They are interested in learning more."
Strong: "This company is expanding its project portfolio and is looking for ways to improve visibility across teams. They currently manage this process manually, and the operations team identified improving efficiency as a priority. They'd like to explore what options exist."

Set the expectation for the prospect too — something like "Based on what you shared, it'd make sense to connect you with [AE], who works with organizations like yours and can dig into your goals in more detail." That one sentence is often what prevents a no-show.

17Objection Handling

Outbound means starting conversations with people who weren't necessarily looking for one, so objections are baked into the job — "we're already using something," "we're too busy," "send me information," "we're not looking," "call me next year." None of these automatically mean there's no opportunity. More often they mean the value of the conversation isn't clear yet, the timing feels off, or the prospect is protecting their time from what looks like a generic pitch. Section 3 covers the mindset for handling rejection in general; this chapter is the tactical layer — what to actually say when a specific objection comes up.

Stay Curious, Not Defensive

The instinctive move is to immediately counter the objection, which usually starts a debate instead of a conversation:

Prospect: "We're already using another platform."
Weak: "Actually, Trimble is better because…"
Better: "That makes sense. Many organizations we speak with already have processes in place. I'm curious, how is your current approach working for your team today?"

A Framework for Any Objection

Acknowledge ("that makes sense," "I appreciate you sharing that") without agreeing there's no opportunity — it's about respect, not concession. Clarify what's actually behind the objection ("can I ask what led you to that?"). Explore whether a real business challenge or opportunity exists ("are there any areas you'd like to improve?"). Advance to whatever's appropriate — continued discovery, an AE conversation, a resource, or a professional close if there's genuinely no fit right now.

Common Objections

ObjectionWhat It May Actually MeanBetter Response
"We're already using something."Satisfied, or switching feels like too much effort"That makes sense. How is that working for your team today?" Then: what do they like most, and is there anything they wish worked better?
"We're happy with our current process."
(even if it's manual, or there's no software at all)		Genuinely satisfied, or hasn't yet hit a pain point that would justify a change"What's been the biggest factor in making your current process successful?" A lot of organizations we work with were also comfortable with their process, but started exploring improvements as their team grew — "where do you see the biggest opportunity for efficiency in that workflow?"
"We're too busy."Competing priorities, or the value isn't clear yet"Completely understand. Out of curiosity, what are the biggest priorities your team's focused on right now?" Worth also asking when things tend to settle down, so you know when to circle back.
"Send me information."Wants context without committing time yet"Happy to send something over — to make sure it's relevant, what area are you most interested in?" It's also fair to ask whether they're actively evaluating anything else in the space, or just researching.
"We're not looking."No active initiative or recognized need yet"Understood — a lot of organizations aren't actively looking until there's a reason to. Curious how you're handling [challenge] today?" If you could snap your fingers and fix one part of that workflow, what would it be?
"Call me next year."Genuine future timing, or a polite way to defer"Happy to reconnect then — what's likely to change between now and next year that makes that the right time?" Teams often start researching in Q3 for a Q1 launch — worth asking if that timeline applies to them.
"We don't have budget."Often means no current initiative, or the value isn't clear yet — rarely a hard no"I understand, budget's always a factor. Before we ever talk investment, it's worth seeing if there's a business challenge here worth solving at all. If we find that opportunity, when does your next fiscal cycle begin?" Don't jump to pricing or discounts — establish the problem and its impact first.
"I'm not the right person."Genuinely the wrong contact, or an easy way to end the call"My mistake — could you point me toward whoever typically handles [specific business function]?" Worth also asking if they happen to know that person's current priorities in that area.
"I've already spoken to someone from your company."A prior touch that may or may not have gone anywhere"That's good to know — do you recall who it was, or how long ago?" Then: has [challenge] improved since that conversation, or is it still a priority?
"We just finished a similar project." / "Implementation is too hard."Recent investment already made, or change-fatigue from a rough rollout elsewhere"That's great — sounds like this is a priority area. What's your strategy for [ongoing maintenance, adoption, or measuring results] on that?" If it's an implementation concern: "if we could show you how we handle the heavy lifting there, would that change your perspective?"
"Is this a cold call?"
(hostile opener)		Testing whether you'll be straightforward or evasive"It is — but I only make a handful of these a day, and I wanted to talk with you specifically because of [research point/relevance]. Do you have 30 seconds for me to explain why?"
"Your competitor does this for cheaper." / "I don't see the value."Price is the visible objection, but there's often a real differentiator question underneath it"Price is certainly important. Usually when people move to us from [Competitor], it's because they were struggling with [differentiator] — how is that currently showing up in your workflow?"

Staying Level-Headed

When a prospect pushes back, resist the urge to get defensive, talk faster, or over-explain — pause, listen, and ask instead. Remember they may be mid-crisis, managing competing priorities, or simply skeptical because they field a lot of sales calls. A calm, curious response changes the direction of more conversations than a well-rehearsed rebuttal ever will. If you catch yourself reaching for "we can help with that" or "our solution is different," swap in a question instead — "how are you approaching that today?" or "what's worked well with your current approach?" almost always opens more than it closes.

When to Push and When to Let Go

Keep going when the prospect shares a real challenge, shows curiosity, or timing seems flexible. Step back when they explicitly ask not to be contacted or the conversation clearly isn't going anywhere productive. Professionalism in the moment you let go is what keeps the door open for later.

Before responding to any objection, a quick gut-check: did I acknowledge what they said, stay curious instead of defensive, ask a real follow-up, understand what's actually behind it, and land on a clear next step either way? An objection isn't the end of a conversation — it's usually the start of understanding what the customer actually thinks.

18Multi-Channel Prospecting

Buyers don't engage with sales outreach in one place — an email, a LinkedIn interaction, a voicemail, an event conversation, a colleague's mention all build awareness in different ways. The mistake is treating each channel as its own disconnected activity. Every touch, across every channel, should reinforce the same underlying message: I understand your business, I think there may be an opportunity worth discussing, and I'd value hearing how you're approaching it today.

Why More Than One Channel

Senior leaders and operational teams are already flooded with communication, so a single email is easy to miss — a coordinated combination is more likely to land. Different people also just prefer different formats: some respond to a call, others to a sharp written insight, others to a peer recommendation. And for Mid-Market and Enterprise deals specifically, multiple stakeholders and longer timelines mean the familiarity you build early compounds into something real later.

The Channels

Section 15 already covers how to write for phone, email, LinkedIn, and voicemail — this is about when and why to reach for each one, plus a few channels that don't come up as often.

  • Phone remains the fastest way to create real dialogue — email communicates, but a conversation builds a relationship.
  • Email gives you an asynchronous way to provide context and keep something moving between calls.
  • LinkedIn builds familiarity before you ever ask for time — engage with a prospect's content before messaging them directly.
  • Video is worth the extra effort for strategic accounts, executive outreach, or a follow-up after some engagement already exists; keep it short, personalized, and centered on one clear next step.
  • Events (conferences, webinars, trade shows) create relationship-building moments before, during, and after the event itself — identify target accounts ahead of time and follow up with something specific afterward.
  • Referrals from existing customers, AEs, or partners carry built-in trust; make the ask easy by giving your connector a clear reason and clear value to pass along.
  • Social engagement — commenting thoughtfully, sharing relevant insight — builds credibility passively; the mindset shift is asking "how do I build relationships through this" rather than "how do I sell through this."

How the Channels Work Together

A coordinated sequence for a strategic account might look like: email on day 1 introducing a relevant challenge, a call on day 2 referencing it, LinkedIn connection and engagement on day 3, a call plus voicemail on day 5, a resource-sharing email on day 7, a personalized video on day 10 for strategic accounts specifically, and a final check-in around day 14 on timing and priorities. The specific cadence matters less than the principle: each touch should add something, not just repeat the ask.

For a true Enterprise account, the channel mix often varies by stakeholder even within the same sequence — an executive contact might get a personalized email, LinkedIn engagement, and a video message, while an operations leader gets a phone conversation and an industry-insight email, and a technical user gets workflow-specific messaging and a resource. The account-level message stays connected even as the channel and angle shift by persona.

Matching Effort to Account Tier

Strategic (Tier 1) accounts warrant deep research, custom messaging, multi-threaded engagement, and close AE collaboration. High-potential (Tier 2) accounts warrant persona-based messaging and consistent, research-backed outreach. Broader prospecting relies more on efficient workflows and strong default messaging frameworks than on deep customization per account. (Section 10 has the full account-tiering breakdown.)

Where Multi-Channel Efforts Break Down

MistakeBetter
Treating each channel as a separate, disconnected activityBuild one coordinated strategy across channels
Using every channel without a reasonChoose channels based on the account and persona, not habit
Staying persistent without adding valueEvery touch should carry new context or insight
Giving up after one or two attemptsMost real opportunities need multiple touches to surface

Worth tracking over time: activity (calls, emails, LinkedIn touches, videos sent), engagement (opens, replies, conversations, meetings created), and quality (target-account engagement, persona engagement, actual opportunity creation). A phone call, an email, and a LinkedIn comment each look small in isolation — together, sustained over time, they're what turns cold outreach into an actual relationship.

PART V

Productivity & Execution

19Daily Operating Rhythm

Outbound success runs on discipline, not motivation or whatever time happens to be left over. A full calendar doesn't automatically mean a productive one — you can spend an entire day in meetings, clearing notifications, and updating systems and still create zero pipeline. The activities that actually move the needle are narrower: researching accounts, contacting prospects, having real conversations, following up, and staying in sync with your AE. Everything else is support work.

Own Your Calendar

Your calendar is your sales strategy made visible. If prospecting is always the thing that gets bumped when something else comes up, pipeline creation will always suffer — so treat time for prospecting, research, follow-up, and planning as commitments, not something you'll get to if the day allows it.

BlockUsed For
ProspectingCalls, emails, LinkedIn engagement, account research
Follow-UpResponding to prospects, advancing conversations, completing next steps
Account PlanningTerritory review, strategic account research, AE collaboration
AdministrativeSalesforce updates, task management, reporting

Protecting Prospecting Time

Research, thoughtful messaging, and quality conversations all require focus that constant interruption destroys. Schedule prospecting blocks as recurring commitments rather than waiting for open time to appear, remove distractions during them (limit meetings, silence notifications), and walk in already knowing which accounts, which personas, and which message you're using — deciding that in the moment burns the block itself.

A Sample Day (Pacific Time)

This is built around one goal — booking high-quality meetings — using the core tool stack (Salesforce, Gong, ZoomInfo, Sales Navigator, Prokeys). Times shift with your own territory and time zone coverage, but the shape underneath it holds up well: two protected call blocks in the morning while operations and field leaders are reachable, research and CRM work filling the gaps, and a lighter "golden hour" pass in the afternoon for reconnects.

TimeBlockDetails & Best Practices
7:15 – 7:30 amMorning SetupLog into Salesforce, review top accounts, listen to one Gong call, set three key goals for the day.
7:30 – 9:30 amCall Block #1 (Prime Time)Cold calls and follow-ups to field and operations leaders. Prioritize ZoomInfo leads; update Salesforce notes in real time.
9:30 – 10:00 amCRM Follow-UpsComplete overdue tasks in Salesforce/Gong. Send recap emails from morning connections.
10:00 – 11:00 amResearch & PersonalizationUse Sales Navigator and ZoomInfo to find 5–10 new targets. Add notes and tags for future sequencing.
11:00 am – 12:00 pmCall Block #2Target PMs and Ops Managers who start later — keep time zones in mind. A mix of cold and follow-up calls.
12:00 – 12:45 pmLunchAway from the desk. Actually recharge.
12:45 – 2:15 pmSequence & Email BlockGong flows and one-offs. Emails to harder-to-reach targets; watch for engagement activity.
2:15 – 3:30 pmCall Block #3 (Golden Hour)Reconnect with aging prospects or pipeline reactivations — shorter, 45-minute bursts.
3:30 pm onwardResearch & PersonalizationSales Navigator and ZoomInfo again, this time for 10+ new targets. Tag and note for tomorrow's sequencing.

Best Practices for the Day

  • Prioritize quality conversations. Pull a Gong snippet into your recap emails — referencing something specific from the actual call builds more credibility than a generic follow-up.
  • Leverage ZoomInfo early. Morning is the right window to confirm contact data before it feeds your first call block.
  • Use Sales Navigator midday. It's the better tool for spotting new buying centers or project-related contacts once you've warmed up on calls.
  • Protect prime time. Keep admin work and non-essential meetings out of your call blocks entirely — this is the same discipline covered above in Protecting Prospecting Time, just applied to specific hours.
  • End strong. The last research block of the day is what tomorrow's first call block runs on — don't let it be the first thing that slips.

Follow-Up as a Discipline, Not an Afterthought

Many opportunities only materialize after the first interaction — a non-response is usually about timing or bandwidth, not disinterest. Every follow-up should add something ("just checking in" adds nothing; a relevant insight, example, or sharper question does), stay persistent without becoming annoying, and always close with a real next step rather than trailing off.

Managing Your Queue

Between new prospects, active sequences, follow-ups, and AE priorities, it's easy to lose track of what actually matters most today. A workable priority order: active conversations first (anyone who replied or showed engagement gets immediate attention), then high-priority accounts (strong ICP fit, live buying signals), then routine sequence tasks, then administrative work last — not because it doesn't matter, but because it doesn't create pipeline on its own.

Weekly Planning

Daily execution holds up better when it's connected to a weekly view: which accounts are moving, what's in the pipeline and how it's progressing, how activity and engagement rates are trending, and what next week's priorities should be. Section 14 covers the joint version of this done together with your AE — this is the version you run on your own first, so you show up to that conversation with an actual point of view.

The Weekly Account Cadence

Where the daily schedule above governs your hours, this governs how a single priority account gets worked over five days. It's the same multi-threading and stakeholder-mapping discipline from Section 11, laid out on a calendar.

DayThemeActions
MondayResearch & LaunchReview the website, LinkedIn, Salesforce, and recent company news. Identify 3–5 stakeholders and build the account map (who's who). Call the primary contact and send Personalized Email #1.
TuesdayMulti-ThreadFollow up with the primary contact. Call and email the secondary contact. Begin outreach to additional stakeholders identified Monday.
WednesdayProvide ValueSend a value-add email — a case study, customer story, webinar, or industry insight. Call active contacts. Expand into another department if the account map suggests one.
ThursdayExecutive OutreachIf there's been no engagement yet, reach out to an executive-level stakeholder. Continue following up with existing contacts, and ask for a referral to the right person where it fits naturally.
FridayReview & Next StepsConfirm every key stakeholder has actually been worked, not just queued. Close out remaining outreach for the week. Schedule the next follow-up, or recycle the account if the week produced nothing to build on.

This is a template, not a script — a strong Tuesday reply can pull Thursday's executive outreach earlier, and a dead week is a legitimate reason to recycle on Friday rather than force a sixth day of silence.

Protecting Focus Time

Prospecting is cognitively demanding — real research, real personalization, real strategic thinking, and constant context-switching quietly erodes all three. Clear your environment before a focus block (fewer open tabs, notifications off), start with a specific goal rather than a vague intention ("engage 15 priority contacts across five strategic accounts," not "prospect for a while"), and take a minute afterward to note what worked and what you'd adjust.

Activity Isn't the Same as Productivity

A hundred generic emails often produce less pipeline than twenty thoughtful, personalized conversations. The rough formula worth internalizing: strategy + consistency + focus + quality = pipeline. Drop any one of the four and the other three can't fully compensate.

Where This Breaks Down

MistakeFix
Prospecting only when free time appearsProtect the block; pipeline becomes inconsistent otherwise
Doing easy administrative tasks firstDo revenue-generating work before it, not after
Letting follow-up slideA disciplined follow-up process is where a lot of opportunity actually lives
Overloading the calendar with meetingsProtect focus blocks like any other commitment

A quick end-of-day check: did I engage priority accounts, create real conversations, close out important follow-ups, update Salesforce, and set up tomorrow? Pipeline is built from small, consistent actions repeated daily — a disciplined rhythm is what turns that into something predictable.

20Technology Stack

A tool doesn't create pipeline — you do, by choosing the right accounts, understanding real challenges, and following through. Technology just provides leverage on top of that. The outbound stack breaks down by function: research (ZoomInfo, LinkedIn, company sites, industry resources — covered in depth in Section 12), engagement (Gong Engage, email, LinkedIn), enablement (Seismic), and intelligence (Salesforce DX, Gong).

Salesforce DX

This is the shared system of record for accounts, contacts, leads, opportunities, and activity — and it matters because accurate data is what lets you and your AE actually collaborate, lets managers see real pipeline health, and gives customers a consistent experience regardless of who they're talking to at Trimble. Section 22 covers exactly what a quality note looks like and what belongs in the record at handoff — the standard there applies to daily updates too, not just the moment of handoff. Update in real time rather than relying on memory; details that feel obvious right after a call are much harder to reconstruct a week later.

Gong

Conversation intelligence for improving how you actually sound on calls — recordings, insights, and coaching. Review your own calls regularly and ask honestly: did I create curiosity, ask strong questions, actually understand their priorities? It's also worth reviewing strong calls from teammates, and worth listening for how customers describe their own problems — their language is often sharper and more usable in your messaging than anything you'd write from scratch.

Gong Engage

The execution layer for structured outbound — multi-channel sequences, persona-based campaigns, task prioritization, and engagement tracking. It's a force multiplier for a good strategy and a noise machine for a bad one: avoid adding prospects without a real reason, avoid generic sequence messaging, and review what's actually working rather than treating it as fire-and-forget. Section 18 covers how to think about sequencing itself; this is the tool that runs it.

A few habits that make it work better day to day: add notes to the Person or Account record so relevant context is right in front of you the next time you call, rather than buried in memory. Use To-Dos to schedule future tasks so a prospect who isn't ready today doesn't quietly fall through the cracks. If no existing Flow fits a specific scenario, don't force it — build a sequence of To-Dos instead, effectively creating your own one-off flow for that person. And the moment you land an SAO, remove every other prospect at that company from cold Flows (Section 22 has the full booking checklist this belongs to) — if it's a good fit, send the other contacts a short email, with your new champion cc'd, inviting them to join the Intro Call.

Seismic

The library for approved sales collateral, product resources, and competitive information. The job isn't finding something to send — it's finding the right resource for this challenge, this role, and this stage of the conversation. More content isn't more helpful past a certain point.

Charlie

Internal knowledge and company updates — useful for staying current on announcements, enablement resources, and anything else worth knowing that isn't customer-facing.

Connecting the Stack

The real value shows up when these tools work together rather than in isolation. A typical flow: identify a target account (Salesforce, ZoomInfo, LinkedIn) to confirm fit and contacts, research the opportunity (Gemini, LinkedIn, industry resources) to find a real business challenge, build the outreach strategy (Gong Engage, Gemini, Seismic) to personalize the approach, engage the prospect (Gong Engage, LinkedIn, Gong) to create an actual conversation, and document and collaborate (Salesforce, Gong) to capture what you learned and support the AE partnership. Section 22 walks through a much more detailed, hands-on version of this exact workflow specifically for ZoomInfo, Salesforce, and Gong Engage together — worth reading in full once you're ready to go deep on execution.

21Tech Stack Workflows

Whether you're receiving targeted lists directly from your AEs or building them out yourself from scratch, prospecting at Trimble requires navigating a robust ecosystem of data and automation. Our tech stack is packed with powerful platforms, and while there's no single "right" way to run a sales cycle, there is a core set of best practices that will make your workflow highly efficient.

This chapter focuses on the integrated tech stack workflow for Salesforce, ZoomInfo, Sales Navigator, and Gong Engage — and more importantly, how to use them together to maximize your pipeline and eliminate wasted effort.

Reports Worth Pulling From Salesforce Into ZoomInfo

The most seamless workflows begin by pulling existing data out of Salesforce to manipulate it inside ZoomInfo.

ReportWhat It Is
AE's Target Account ListHigh-priority, net-new accounts assigned to your territory that your AE wants prioritized for strategic outbound
Closed-Lost ListAccounts that fell out of the funnel 6–12 months ago due to timing, budget, or a competitor — now ripe for re-engagement
Stalled Inbound / Historical MPL ListPast hand-raisers, webinar attendees, or high-intent content downloaders from the last 6–12 months who went cold or never progressed to an active opportunity
Corporate Hierarchy Whitespace ReportEnterprise accounts where Trimble has landed in one regional office or subsidiary (e.g., Texas Civil Division) — pull into ZoomInfo to map and expand into the rest of the parent company's divisions
ERP ProspectsExisting customers using a single Trimble product (e.g., Accubid or ProjectSight) but running a generic, legacy ERP for back-office accounting — prime targets for Trimble Construction One bundles including Vista or Spectrum
"Hardware-Only" (SaaS Cross-Sell) ReportExisting customers who own Trimble physical assets (robotic total stations, fleet telematics, machine control) but have zero cloud software or subscription SaaS licenses attached

The Ultimate Goal: Running Strategic Plays

So what do you do if your AE sends you a list of accounts in Salesforce with a G-Chat message saying "go for it!"? Your immediate reaction shouldn't be to start blindly cold-calling. To protect your efficiency and find the highest-probability buyers, systematically narrow that list down so only your absolute "good fits" remain — with one goal in mind: running highly targeted sales plays.

What is a "sales play"? At Trimble, a sales play is a repeatable, coordinated outreach strategy — combining phone calls, custom emails, and LinkedIn touches — triggered by a specific business event, tech stack signal, or customer scenario. A play is the opposite of generic, "spray-and-pray" prospecting: it lets you approach a specific persona, speak directly to the pain point they're facing today, and present a tailored value proposition that feels warm, timely, and hyper-relevant.

Layering the Three Elements of a "Good Fit"

  • Good-fit accounts: Filter the AE's list against your target criteria — are they in your territory, and do they match the employee size, Gross Annual Revenue (GAR), and NAICS codes for your ICP? (If unsure what a good account looks like, reverse-engineer recent closed-won accounts.)
  • Good-fit contacts: Filter for the precise buying-committee personas with the right titles. For Civil, that's VP of Operations, Survey Manager, Chief Estimator, GPS Coordinators.
  • Good-fit contact info: Filter results to only show contacts with verified direct-dial phone numbers and business emails.

Strategic Multi-Threading: Customer vs. New Logo

To break into or expand an account, you can never rely on a single contact — but your pacing, depth, and volume change entirely based on account type.

Account TypeStrategy
Customer Expansion (Go Wide & Fast)Multi-thread aggressively — 10+ stakeholders across departments simultaneously. Strategy is cross-selling complementary product lines (e.g., pitching cloud software to a team that only owns hardware).
New Logo Outbound (Go Deep & Targeted)Minimize research time to maximize speed. Isolate 3–4 hyper-specific personas (e.g., Chief Estimator, VP of Operations, GPS Manager) and hit them with coordinated, simultaneous touches to spark a first internal conversation.

By cleaning, filtering, and mapping accounts up front, you turn a messy spreadsheet of company names into a laser-targeted list of active decision-makers — and the data tells you your exact angle instead of you having to guess.

Tech Stack Workflow

Step 1: Export List From Salesforce to ZoomInfo

Before launching any cold outreach, pull your targets from Salesforce — an AE-provided list or a self-sourced report like a Closed-Lost sweep — and export it as a CSV file (Details Only).

Step 2: Bulk Prospecting via ZoomInfo ListMatch

Import your Salesforce report to ZoomInfo:
  Left sidebar -> Lists and Records -> Lists -> Upload Lists ->
  Companies -> ListMatch -> Upload CSV file

Weed out bad data:
  During upload, filter out companies with no verified website
  (under "Mapping" -> Company URL)

Expand the search, once the list is processed:
  - Click "Open in Search" to push accounts into Advanced Search
    and apply persona filters (Industry: Heavy Civil, Construction;
    Job Titles: VP of Operations, Chief Estimator)
  - OR click "Generate Lookalikes" to find new, similar accounts
    based on recent closed-won criteria

Step 3: Advanced Filtering & Building Saved Searches

Combine multiple filters to isolate high-probability buyers:

FilterUse
FirmographicsLocation (strictly aligned to territory), employee count, GAR requirements
Corporate HierarchySelect "Parent Companies Only" to target the primary decision-making entity
NAICS CodesAccurately map accounts to specific geographic verticals
Personas & Buying GroupsFilter by job titles and pre-built corporate buying groups
"Likely to Engage"Prioritize prospects who historically respond to outreach or are active on LinkedIn
TechnologiesSearch for companies using competitive or complementary software (e.g., Procore) — enables a Tech Displacement play (from a Closed-Lost list) or a Tech Integration play
ScoopsReal-time corporate intelligence and event triggers — executive switches, contract wins, budget updates, operational pain points
Salesforce IntegrationFilter by account owner to avoid stepping on toes, or exclude companies already in Salesforce when hunting net-new logos
Your strategy flips depending on the playbook: New Logo hunters use the Salesforce filter defensively to wipe out existing accounts and see only uncontacted space. Customer SDRs do the opposite — isolating current accounts while filtering out reps outside their assigned territory.

Get creative with filters — there's no silver bullet:

  • Keyword manipulation: search niche terms like "BIM compliance," "autonomous grading," "telematics," or "3D modeling" instead of standard industry filters.
  • The reverse filter: exclude your standard filters for a day to see what falls through the cracks; if a combination yields zero results, tweak it.
  • The "under-teched" filter: search for large-revenue companies ($100M+) with shockingly low employee counts — usually means heavy reliance on subs or a real need for automation.

Step 4: Leveraging Sales Signals — Intent & Scoops

Intent data is a digital reverse-lookup: it tracks when an account is doing an abnormal amount of research into topics relevant to Trimble. A spike means they've moved past awareness and are actively in a buying cycle.

Building the intent search: select topics (broad bundles like Cloud ERP, or narrower ones like Construction Accounting Software), filter by industry and territory to keep the list clean, and set the date range — last 30 days for a broader view, last 7 days for the hottest signals.

Customer Expansion tip: if a customer rep recently sold Tekla to a Mid-Market or Enterprise account, pull that account into the intent panel and check whether they're researching ERP or financial suites. Construction ERP migrations are massive, high-dollar deals — catching an existing customer researching accounting software is the wedge to introduce Trimble Construction One before a competitor gets in.

Drilling down: select the whole page of spiking companies, click "Open in Advanced Search," pivot to the Contacts tab, and filter for the actual decision-makers (Estimators, CEOs, CFOs). Save the search and check it every morning to catch territory accounts heating up in real time.

Executing on intent: these accounts need a different operational playbook — don't drop them into a standard 30-day sequence. Run a compressed, high-velocity flow (more dials, shorter gaps) to book the meeting before the buying window closes. If a few weeks of high-velocity outreach gets zero response, pull them out and drop them into a long-term nurture instead of burning more energy.

The golden rule of intent messaging: don't be creepy. Never reveal your source.

Creepy: "Hey, I saw you guys were looking at ERP Solutions online, so I wanted to call…"

Strategic: "Hey John, a lot of CFOs in the heavy civil space tell us that as they scale, their biggest bottleneck is manual data re-entry between estimating and back-office accounting. I know operations visibility is a major focus for teams like yours right now. How are you currently bridging the gap between the field and your financial systems?"

Use the intent data to form a strategic assumption and write as if it's a happy coincidence — hit the exact problem they're solving for without making them feel watched.

Scoops let you read between the lines of corporate announcements to reverse-engineer contextual sales angles.

TriggerAssumptionHook
Management shifts (new VP of Operations, CIO, Director of VDC)New leaders carry a mandate to overhaul inefficient processes and fresh budget allocation — the 30–90 day onboarding window is the golden target"Congrats on taking the reins as [Title] at [Company]. Typically, when stepping into a new operations leadership role, identifying data silos between field hardware and office platforms is a top priority. We help incoming leaders benchmark their tech stack…"
M&A / capital infusionGrowth mandates create operational chaos — merged companies inherit different tech stacks and messy data silos"Usually, when heavy civil firms merge, the biggest headache is standardizing field data across different crews. We help unified teams consolidate their workflows into a single cloud ecosystem…"
Major project / contract winImmediate time crunch with thin margins — public infrastructure carries heavy financial penalties for delays"With margins as tight as they are on public infrastructure, any rework or manual data transfer is a profit killer. Let's look at how our machine control solutions ensure you hit grade right the first time."
"Digital transformation" / tech budgetPre-approved budget is carved out, and leadership is forcing a shift from legacy, paper-based workflows"A lot of operations leaders find the hardest part of going digital is connecting actual field hardware assets to the back office. We specialize in building that direct bridge…"
Aggressive field hiringScaling pains and labor shortages — training a wave of new field workers on fragmented tools leads to error"When bringing on a wave of new field engineers, manual errors usually spike. We help rapidly growing teams standardize field workflows with intuitive software that gets new hires productive in days."
Layoffs / downsizingRemaining staff is overworked and must do more with less"When teams are forced to do more with less, manual data re-entry is a massive bottleneck. We help lean operations teams automate field-to-office data streams…"

Step 5: Power Duo — LinkedIn Sales Navigator + ZoomInfo Chrome Extension

Sales Navigator is your source of truth for org charts and professional movement. ZoomInfo is your database for verified contact data and company intelligence. Paired together: use LinkedIn for precise targeting and relationship mapping while ZoomInfo fills the gaps with verified emails, direct dials, and company-level intelligence. (Prerequisite: the ZoomInfo Chrome Extension.)

Navigating a company profile: "All Employees" gives a real-time, accurate list of who's actually there — use it to map the full field and office ecosystem. "Decision Makers" is a quick macro-filter for leadership, but cross-reference it with "All Employees" so you don't miss key influencers or hidden field champions.

High-speed live scan workflow:
1. Keep your Sales Navigator search or account page open, with
   the ZoomInfo Chrome Extension overlay running alongside it
2. Work down the LinkedIn list line by line -- the extension
   overlays ZoomInfo's data on top of LinkedIn, revealing verified
   direct dials and business emails without leaving the page
3. From the extension pane, push contacts and the mapped buying
   committee directly into Salesforce or Gong Flows

Saved searches worth setting up: a "New Executive" alert (target titles + "changed jobs in the last 90 days"), and a "New Field Leader" alert (Senior PMs or Survey Managers with "Past Company = [key competitors or Trimble customers]," checked every Monday to catch them during onboarding).

How Do You Know You're Targeting the Right Accounts?

Judge a book by its cover. High-yield prospecting requires execution viability before you ever pick up the phone — visually inspect company names, target titles, and website projects/imagery to confirm real-world fit against your ICP. And audit data density: a seemingly perfect Tier 1 account with no direct dials or verified emails is a data ghost town an SDR can't actually break into. A "data-rich" account — dense, clean contact data across multiple personas — is always the premium target.

Lets Walk Through an Example: Armstrong Infrastructure Partners

You support the Civil vertical. Your AE hands you an account list; Armstrong Infrastructure Partners is first up.

  1. Company name & messaging: look for keywords like Earthworks, Grading, Heavy Civil, Highway, Utilities, Excavation, Paving. Their homepage reads "Specializing in site preparation and mass excavation" — confirmed Civil target, not a vertical building contractor.
  2. Website photos: check the Projects/Gallery page for heavy machinery, highways, bridges, deep utility trenches. Their gallery shows a fleet of CAT excavators digging a retention pond — an ideal target for Trimble Machine Control (Earthworks) and Site Positioning Systems.
  3. Persona titles (the smoking gun): search "About Us" or LinkedIn Sales Nav for titles unique to civil workflows — Survey Manager, Chief Estimator, Grade Superintendent, GPS Manager/Coordinator. You find "Dale," GPS/Insite Coordinator — the title alone tells you this company already uses 3D models and automated machine guidance. Tech-forward.
  4. LinkedIn deep-dive: a lot of targets have websites that look like they're from 1999, with no social links attached. If you find a name (say, the Head of Estimating) but no LinkedIn link, Google the exact phrase — "Joe Smith New England Earthworks LinkedIn." Once found, mine the profile: recent posts (proof you did your homework), career history (did they come from a Trimble customer? trigger the Champion Tracking play), and mutual connections or shared groups for rapport.

The result changes the outreach entirely — instead of a generic "Trimble software" email:

"Dale, I saw the team recently wrapped up that mass excavation project on Highway 80. Looking at your role as GPS Coordinator, I know how brutal it is to manually fix 3D model errors when the field design changes mid-day. I wanted to show you how we hook Trimble Business Center directly into the field…"

Step 6: The Export & Execution Workflow (ZoomInfo → Salesforce → Gong)

Once your data is clean and signals are locked in, push accounts into active sequences without losing momentum. The export path depends on whether the contact already exists in Salesforce.

Scenario A — New leads and contacts, not yet in Salesforce:

Simultaneous export via ZoomInfo Extension:
1. Identify the new leads/contacts and open the ZoomInfo Extension
2. Push leads, contacts, and the mapped buying committee directly
   into Salesforce from the extension
3. Simultaneously, send the contacts directly to Gong Engage,
   bypassing manual Salesforce routing

Scenario B — Contacts already in Salesforce (cannot be added to a Gong flow directly from ZoomInfo — must route through Salesforce first):

First: Export from ZoomInfo to Salesforce
1. Check the boxes next to target contacts in ZoomInfo
2. Click Export -> select Salesforce from the dropdown
3. Choose Leads or Contacts (if Contacts, map to the correct
   existing Account)
4. Review any duplicate alerts, then Export

Second: Push to Gong Flows via Salesforce
1. Open the Account, Lead list, or Contact list you just imported
2. Select the newly imported prospects
3. Click the Gong Chrome Extension icon (or "Add to Gong" in the
   Salesforce UI)
4. Select "Add to Flow" and choose the flow matching your trigger
   (if no matching flow exists, talk to your manager about
   creating one)

Multi-threading once contacts are live in flows: top-down — call the ultimate decision-maker first; even on voicemail, you can then call their direct reports and reference having just reached out to the executive. Bottom-up — call end-users or direct reports first to gather ground-level insight, then thread up to the executive using that leverage. The blueprint either way: good-fit account, layered with good-fit contacts (right titles), layered with accurate contact info (mobile numbers).

Parting Thought: Data Cleansing Is Prospecting

It's easy to treat data filtering, list cleaning, and account mapping as administrative overhead — a chore before the "real work." Flip that: the meticulous effort spent fixing, filtering, and refining your database right now is what saves you hundreds of wasted dials and dead ends later. Clean data is the high-leverage foundation pipeline gets built on.

Make it a non-negotiable habit to fill the gaps — hunt down missing names within the account hierarchy, map the buying committee to exact validated titles, and lock in direct dials and verified emails before a contact ever touches a sequence.

Data is a guide, not absolute truth. No platform is perfect — algorithms occasionally misclassify accounts or surface an outdated title. Don't let rigid parameters box you in. Treat the tech stack like a sandbox: experiment with filters, run keyword experiments, and adapt based on what's actually working on the phones. The elite SDRs don't just follow the data blindly — they use it as a launchpad to hunt creatively.

The Standard Outbound Process

Whichever report you're working from on a given day, the process underneath it stays the same:

  1. Access your current document. Open the report or list you're working today, and confirm you have everything you need — the right filters, the right tools open — before you start dialing.
  2. Apply filters. Narrow the list by Representative or by State, depending on whether your strategy that day is rep-specific or territory-specific.
  3. Engage with leads. Review the filtered list and identify the ones that actually show potential, then run a simple four-touch flow: call to make a personal connection (if there's no answer, redial once — a "double tap" — before moving on), email to follow up and reinforce the message, reply to anything the lead sends back to keep the conversation alive, then call again to further the relationship and discuss next steps.
