Closed Won ReportWarmCross-sell based on ROE, additional licenses

The Closed Lost Report here is the same report referenced as the master shell template in the Closed-Lost Re-engagement play in Section 23 — clone it from this link rather than hunting for it separately.

One More LinkedIn Habit

Beyond the saved-search alerts covered above: whatever you find on a prospect's profile — a recent post, a shared connection, a previous employer — actually use it in your outreach. Noticing it and not mentioning it wastes the research.

Create & Complete the Lead Record

Salesforce DX is where every lead's journey actually gets recorded, so it's worth knowing the mechanics cold. Start here: get the lead into the system and every required field filled in before you do anything else — a complete record is what drives accurate routing, ownership assignment, and reporting for whoever engages this prospect next, including you a few steps from now.

1. Create the Lead (If It Doesn't Already Exist)

Creating an account from a lead happens through the lead conversion process, and should happen once a lead is actually ready to enter the pipeline as an opportunity. If the lead isn't already in Salesforce as an MPL or SRL, create it yourself as a new lead — but confirm a duplicate doesn't already exist first. Then open the Leads tab on the homescreen and select New Lead.

2. Fill In the Required Fields

When you create a lead manually, every required Salesforce field has to be completed — this is what drives accurate routing, ownership assignment, reporting, and future opportunity creation. The more complete the record, the easier it is for whoever engages this prospect next.

Required to create the lead: First & Last Name, Company, Email, Country Code, State, Lead Source, Job Role, Sector (CES – Construction), Product Category, and Gross Annual Revenue (GAR).

Two more fields become required before you can convert the lead, even though they aren't required to create it: Phone Number and Complete Address. Get them on the record early so conversion doesn't stall later.

Salesforce DX to Gong Engage: Putting a Lead Into a Flow

Once a lead exists in Salesforce DX, the next step is getting it in front of the prospect. That happens in Gong Engage, not Salesforce. Adding the lead to a flow starts the outreach cadence; it does not by itself mean the lead is qualified. Only after you've made contact and qualified them does the Account Verification process below come into play.

1. Open the Lead in Gong Engage

Log into the Gong Sandbox and use the Engage dropdown on the left-hand side to select People.

2. Find the Lead and Add to Flow

In the People tab, select Leads (or Contacts) to pull up the record you just created in Salesforce DX — use the search bar if it doesn't appear right away. Once you've found them, click Add to flow to start engaging.

3. Choose the Right Prospecting Flow

A pop-up lists the available flows. Select the appropriate prospecting flow by clicking on it to add the lead.

A confirmation banner appears once the lead has been successfully added to the selected flow.

The lead's Flow status changes to In flow, and the next flow action — typically Write an Email — appears in the Actions column.

Added the lead to the wrong flow? Click In flow to open the Manage flows pop-up, select Remove next to the flow, then click Save to confirm before adding them to the correct one.

4. Manage Flow Actions Through To-Dos

You can add leads to flows directly from the People tab, but you'll spend most of your time in To-Dos managing the leads you've already added. From the To-Dos tab under Engage, locate the lead and click the task on the right — in this example, Write email.

5. Complete the Step and Send

Clicking the task opens the pre-populated content for that step of the flow — in this case, the first email. Make any necessary edits and click Send.

6. Track Engagement and Complete the Flow

Once a step is complete, the next flow action appears along with its due date, and the lead's Activity feed starts showing your outreach so you can keep track of engagement with them going forward.

Continue working the steps — calls, auto emails, LinkedIn connects — in the order the flow lays them out until the whole sequence is complete.

Compliance, Duplicate Handling & Conversion

Once the lead has been worked and qualified through Gong Engage, it's time to prepare it for conversion. This is the click-by-click version of the process referenced in Section 22's handoff walkthrough: running the compliance check every net-new account needs, catching duplicates before they become a mess, and converting the lead into a Contact, Account, and Opportunity.

1. Run the Secretary of State (SOS) Compliance Check

Before converting, confirm the business is an actively registered corporate entity — this protects Trimble from fraud and bad data, and it's required on every net-new account, not just the ones that look questionable.

  • Navigate to the official Secretary of State (SOS) business entity registry for the state where the company is headquartered — U.S. Secretary of State Search, or Canada's Business Registries Search for Canadian companies.
  • Click through to the state's registry page and enter the company's full legal name into the search field.
  • Cross-reference and verify the Legal Entity Name and Registered Address exactly match what's on the lead in Salesforce, then choose the correct company from the results.
  • Print or export the official registry lookup page as a PDF — make sure it includes the company name and address.
Heads up on Canada and New Jersey specifically: those government registries won't show a company's address without payment — plan for that before you're mid-verification on a call.

Once the Salesforce Account exists, upload that PDF to its Notes & Attachments section — that's the compliance evidence the Customer Master team needs before they'll approve the record.

2. Match the Lead to the SOS Cert, Then Convert

Before converting, update the Company Name and full Address on the lead so they exactly match the SOS cert — including proper capitalization and punctuation. Once Name, Title, Email, Phone, Job Role, Sector, GAR, and Product Category are all filled in, confirm you're the lead's owner (or use the head-with-arrows icon next to the Lead Owner field to reassign it to yourself), confirm no duplicates exist, and click Convert at the top of the record.

This is what a lead record looks like whether you created it manually or it arrived as an MPL/SRL — Convert lives in the top-right corner.

3. Handle Duplicate Warnings

Salesforce checks for duplicates at multiple points on its own. If a lead shares an email address with another lead or contact already in the system, a gray warning bar appears across the top of the record. When you convert a lead that looks like a possible duplicate, Salesforce surfaces the matching record(s) so you can select them instead of creating a new one.

If a duplicate account exists but its name or address isn't correct, don't create a separate account — choose the suggested/duplicate account, then file a request with the Customer Master team to fix the name or address.

4. Create — or Choose Existing — Account, Contact & Opportunity

Once you click Convert, you'll choose to create a new Account, Contact, and Opportunity, or — if matches already exist in Salesforce — select them instead via the "Choose Existing" option on each.

Creating all three fresh — the default when nothing already exists in Salesforce.

Selecting an existing Account and Contact instead — review the match carefully before confirming it.

Always create the Opportunity if you can. It's best practice to create an Opportunity directly from the lead conversion whenever possible, since this is what gets tracked in Marketing Cloud and other reporting systems. Converting a viable lead without creating an Opportunity breaks the connection between the lead and the opportunity and can cause a real loss of data.

One more thing worth knowing: leads entered into Salesforce manually are not automatically added into Marketing campaigns.

5. Confirm the Conversion & Prep the Account for Sync

Once converted, you can jump straight to the new Account, Contact, and Opportunity records from the confirmation screen. If the account hasn't been synced yet, enter the appropriate information there and kick off the upgrade process so it can be synced by the correct team.

Putting It All Together: The Quick Checklist

  1. Document all activity on the lead.
  2. Verify the company name and address on the call — this matters especially in Canada and New Jersey, where the government registries won't show an address without payment.
  3. Pull the SOS cert (or Canadian registry page) and save it as a PDF that includes the company name and address.
  4. Update the Company Name and full Address on the lead to exactly match the SOS cert before converting — proper capitalization and punctuation included.
  5. Complete the required fields: Name, Title, Email, Phone, Job Role, Sector, GAR, Product Category.
  6. Convert the lead — click the radials to create an Opportunity, a Contact, and an Account.

Account Verification: Getting the New Account Synced

Converting the lead only gets the Account record created — it still enters Salesforce in an unapproved state. Before anyone can create a quote against it, the Account has to clear a validation process called syncing, managed by the corporate Customer Master team. Here's what that involves and how to get a new Account through it cleanly.

1. Understand What Syncing Actually Does

An unsynced Account can't have quotes created against it, so syncing isn't optional busywork — it's what unlocks the rest of the sales process. Syncing is what:

  • Creates the Account in Oracle and the Customer Data Hub (CDH)
  • Triggers the compliance check and credit check on the Account
  • Validates the tax status of any tax IDs on the Account
  • Locks certain fields so critical information can't get changed in one system without the other staying in sync
This verification runs on a strict 24–48 hour SLA — plan your prospect follow-up around that window rather than assuming it's instant.

2. Know What the Red Error Messages Mean

If you create an Opportunity on an Account that hasn't been synced yet, you'll see red error messages on the Opportunity — a missing Enterprise Customer ID, a missing Enterprise Address ID on the Billing or Shipping Address, a missing Enterprise Contact ID, no Invoice Recipient, and so on.

This is okay. Once the Account is synced and you update the address details on the Opportunity, these errors clear on their own. For help resolving a specific Enterprise ID error, there's a job aid for that: Correcting Enterprise ID Errors.

3. Get the Three Pieces in Place Before Requesting a Sync

An Account is only ready to sync once all three of these are in place:

  • Billing/Shipping Address — an active Contact Point Address (CPA) of each type
  • Invoice Recipient Contact — at least one Contact marked with that role
  • Territory — assigned per your team's territory routing rules

Only request a sync when there's an actual viable sales opportunity behind the Account. If it's not time to work the opportunity yet, leave the Account unsynced rather than pushing it through prematurely.

4. Verify & Lock In the Account Name

Whether the Account was created through lead conversion or directly, you have to verify the prospect or customer's legal name is correct — using an official registration database (Secretary of State sites in the U.S., Companies House in the UK). You can still edit the Account Name up until it's synced to Oracle and CDH; after that, it's locked, and any correction has to go through a case to the Customer Master team via the Request Change button.

Request Change is how any post-sync correction gets routed to Customer Master — for the name, an address, or anything else that's already locked.

No official name yet? If the customer is still setting up their company, create the Account using "Doing Business As" (DBA) — enter the individual responsible for setting up the company, then DBA followed by the company name expected to be registered. Once the real name is confirmed, request that Customer Master update it via Request Change.

5. Confirm the Account's Addresses (CPAs)

Every Account needs an active billing and shipping address before it can sync — Salesforce calls these Contact Point Addresses (CPA). If the addresses came in automatically through lead conversion, review them: open the Related list on the Account and click into each address record one at a time.

From an address record, click Edit, then click Verify at the bottom of the Edit screen.

Review whatever address suggestions come back, accept the ones that are correct, and click Save.

Don't use commas in address fields. A comma anywhere in an address field interferes with validating that address through the compliance software.

If the Account was created directly — not through lead conversion — and has no address yet, add one using the New Address button, but only before the Account syncs. After that, adding or editing an address requires a Request Change case to Customer Master, same as the Account name.

More detail on addresses in DX lives in the Address Management Job Aid.

6. Set the Invoice Recipient Contact

Every Account needs at least one active Contact marked as the Invoice Recipient — without one, you'll see an error message on the record.

If the right Contact already exists on the Account, open it, go to its Administrative section, and update Contact Operational Role to Invoice Recipient.

If the Account has no Contact at all yet, add one using the New Contact button at the top of the Account.

A Contact can't be moved to a different Account once it's created. Double-check you're adding it to the right Account, especially if there's a parent or other related Account in the hierarchy — and only add actual employees of the Account through the New Contact button.

How to Begin Account Sync

Once you've verified the addresses and updated the related contacts from the steps above, the Account is almost ready to sync — just two more pieces of information stand between you and clicking the button.

1. Assign the Territory

A Territory must be assigned before an Account can sync. Territory assignment is what dictates AE ownership, keeps regional forecasting clean, and routes active pipeline to the right teams — so it has to go through the approved workflow below, not a manual edit.

Do not manually update Territory using Quick Links in Salesforce. Salesforce requires assignment through the approved process so the information updates correctly across every connected system.

Click the dropdown arrow in the upper right of the Account (next to Begin Account Upgrade Process), then select Assign Territory.

2. Work Through the Territory/Branch Drill-Down

The Assign Territory pop-up walks you through a branching set of choices — pick the option that matches the account's business, and each screen narrows the path further until you land on an actual territory code. Here's a full example workflow, start to finish:

Six clicks from branch to territory code — the exact path depends on the account's industry and segment.

Not sure what your AE's code is? The Sales Staff Sheet has the territory code definitions and AE assignments, and the SDR team's SDR/Seller Look-Up Sheet helps you find the right seller and territory code fast — the same sheet referenced back in Section 22.

3. Set the Account Segment

The Account Segment field should match the Territory you just assigned — Major, Strategic, Enterprise, Mid-Market, or SMB. If you're not sure which one applies, select Commercial rather than guessing at a segment.

4. Click Begin Account Upgrade Process

Once the Territory and Account Segment are both set — on top of the address, contact, and name verification from the previous steps — you're ready to actually kick off the sync.

The Account moves into Customer Master Review status, and a case gets created on the Account automatically — that case lands in the Customer Master support queue and is how the whole sync process gets tracked from here.

5. Let the Remaining Stages Run on Their OwnCustomer Master / Systems

Someone from Customer Master, Order Admin, or the Deal Desk will review the Account before finalizing the sync — and from Customer Master Review onward, the remaining stages aren't yours to touch.

Do not try to manually move the Account's status through CDH Customer Check, Compliance, or Tax Exemption. All three are controlled by integrations with other systems, not by hand — trying to force them along just risks the data going out of sync between systems.

Account to Verified Account: Putting It All Together

The same process end to end, as one checklist:

  1. Assign the Territory using the dropdown next to Begin Account Upgrade Process (top right) — this should be the AE's territory.
  2. Add a new address with the New Address button — name it "Registered" or "Primary Address," set the type to Billing, match it exactly to the SOS cert, and check both Default and Shipping.
  3. Attach the SOS cert under Notes and Attachments.
  4. Mark Direct Customer and Credit Line <$50k as "Yes."
  5. Add the Shipping and Billing Contact.
  6. Select the Account Segment (SMB, MM, or ENT) based on GAR.
  7. Mark the Contact as Invoice Recipient on their Contact page.
  8. Click Begin Account Upgrade Process.

Quick visual reference for steps 1–6 above:

1. Assign Territory

2. Add the new address, matched to the SOS cert

3. Attach the SOS cert under Notes & Attachments

4. Mark Direct Customer and Credit Line <$50k as Yes

5. Add the Shipping and Billing Contact

6. Mark the Contact as Invoice Recipient on their Contact page

Opportunity Creation: New Logo

Once the Account is synced (or even before, if you created the Opportunity directly from the lead conversion process), the Opportunity itself still needs its own required fields filled in correctly — this is what actually gets your pipeline counted and forecasted correctly.

There are two different ways to create an Opportunity:

  • Through the lead conversion process — see the Step-by-Step Handoff Process in Section 22 and the Salesforce DX walkthrough earlier in this chapter.
  • By creating an amendment, for an existing customer adding or swapping products — see the Amendments in Salesforce DX guide (the same one referenced in Section 22).

If you're creating the Opportunity after the lead conversion process rather than during it, navigate to the Opportunity on the newly created Account to fill in the rest.

Opportunity — New Logo Required Fields

FieldWhat Goes In It
Close DateSet to 3 months out from the current date
Opportunity NameFollow the naming convention below
StageProspecting / Pursue
Lead SourceChoose the appropriate source from the dropdown
Next StepAdd a date/time and meeting type, e.g. "9/24 10am Intro Discussion"
SectorConstruction
Billing ContactAdd here
Shipping ContactAdd here
Product of InterestMove the appropriate products to the Chosen column
Deal Order TypeNew Logo for a genuinely new account — see the Deal Order Types below for existing customers
TerritoryAdd the AE's and Product Specialist's Territories
  1. Go to Opportunities in the Quick Guide and click New — unless you already created an Opportunity while converting the lead.
  2. Update the Opportunity fields per the table above.
  3. Click Save.
  4. Update the Opportunity Owner to the appropriate Account Executive.

Deal Order Types

  • New Logo — A new account buys a Trimble product for the first time, or after a former customer has been off contract for at least 12 months.
  • Transformation — An existing customer moves from the on-premise or term-license version of a product to the SaaS version of the same product. Any related opportunity removing the replaced product should also be marked Transformation, so the total value of the transaction nets out correctly.
  • Migration — An existing customer moves from a legacy or end-of-life product to its replacement. Same netting logic as Transformation: mark the related opportunity removing the old product as Migration too.
  • Upsell — An existing customer adds additional products, licenses, or capability within a Product Capability they already own.
  • Cross-Sell — An existing customer adds a new Product Capability they don't currently have.
  • Downsell & Renewal — SDRs and sellers do not use this Deal Order Type.

Opportunity Naming Convention

To keep pipeline data clean, format every Opportunity name using this exact pattern:

Company Name – Segment – Product – Quarter/Year
Example: ABC Contracting Inc – MMNL - Vista – Q226

The benefit: standardizing the name lets sales leadership evaluate active pipeline at a glance, monitor deal aging, and keep corporate forecasts clean.

What Comes Next?

Once the lead has been qualified, converted, and the Opportunity has been correctly created and reassigned to the AE, the setup is complete.

From there, the focus shifts from record management to customer transition. The SDR is responsible for ensuring the qualified opportunity is handed to the AE with the context, documentation, meeting setup, and expectations needed to continue the conversation without losing momentum.

Refer to Section 22: AE Handoff & Partnership for the complete handoff process, including:

  • Gold-Level handoff notes
  • AE and Product Seller coordination
  • Discovery meeting scheduling
  • Customer introduction
  • Calendar and Opportunity ownership transfer
  • Internal context transfer
  • Live meeting handoff
  • No-show management
  • AE feedback and post-handoff expectations

22SDR to AE Handoff

A strong handoff of a qualified opportunity from you to an AE should feel like a continuation of the customer conversation. Your job is to give the AE enough context to understand why the customer reached out, what you learned, why it matters, who is involved, and what should happen next.

For the full SDR & AE working model — including ownership, SLAs, follow-up expectations, no-shows, feedback, opportunity progression, escalation paths, and partnership norms — review the SDR & AE Partnership Playbook.

SDR vs. AE Scope Boundaries

Responsibility SDR Scope AE Scope
Primary Goal Respond to prospect interest, understand the need, qualify the opportunity, and create a strong next step Conduct deeper discovery, align the right solution, advance the buying process, and close business
Discovery Establish current state, challenge, impact, stakeholders, urgency, and next-step relevance Deepen discovery around requirements, decision process, solution fit, commercial considerations, and implementation
Customer Communication Own initial response, follow-up, qualification, and meeting coordination Own the sales conversation once the opportunity is accepted and progressing
Handoff Document the customer story, set expectations, and transfer complete context Review SDR context before the meeting and continue from what has already been started
In-Scope Tasks Lead response, discovery, qualification, appropriate multi-threading, CRM documentation, meeting booking, handoff preparation Deeper solution discovery, demos, pricing, proposals, negotiation, security, procurement, and contracting
Out-of-Scope Product feature demos, contract redlines, pricing sheets Ignoring context from SDRs, letting SAOs sit idle without conversion

Standard Gold-Level Handoff Note Template

Use this exact structure when routing a meeting in Salesforce DX and sending context via Google Chat to your AE: 

DATE: 8/25/26
COMPANY: Cheyenne Mechanical Subcontractors (Mid-Market MEP)
CONTACT: Sarah Williams (Estimating Coordinator) & Tom Vance (VP of Operations)
COMPELLING EVENT: Demo request following whitepaper download on AutoBid integration.
ADDRESS: 123 Arapahoe St, Cheyenne, WY
PHONE: 970-555-5555
EMAIL: sarah@cheymech.com
WEB: cheymech.com

CRITICAL BUSINESS ISSUE (PAIN):
Cheyenne is experiencing 2-3 day billing delays per project. Their accounting team manually re-types spreadsheet bid items into their accounting system, causing data typos and unapproved job site work.

BANT QUALIFICATION:
[N] Need: Automate estimation-to-ERP data bridge to eliminate
double-entry.
[A] Authority: Sarah is the end-user evaluator; Tom Vance (VP Ops) has final sign-off and will attend the discovery call. CFO signs contracts.
[B] Budget: Contingency budget available if ROI on labor
time-savings is proven.
[T] Timeline: Needs system selected prior to Q1 project kickoffs.

AREA OF INTEREST: Estimating
- PRIMARY INTEREST (PRODUCTS): AutoBid
- USERS (SCOPE): N/A at this time
- GROSS ANNUAL REVENUE (GAR): $25M
- CURRENT SOFTWARE: PlanSwift

NEXT STEPS:
30-minute Discovery session scheduled for Thursday at 10:00 AM EST (Calendar invite accepted). Sarah is bringing sample job phase spreadsheets to map gaps live.

Required Meeting-Booking Info (minimum bar)

  • What triggered the lead
  • What was discussed
  • What the prospect cares about
  • Calendar standards: agenda, attendees, context attached to the invite

The Five Questions Behind Every Good Handoff

The Gold-Level template above is the structure; these are the questions it's actually answering. If you can't answer all five in a sentence or two, the handoff isn't ready yet: Why did the customer reach out? What problem are they actually trying to solve (not just the product they searched for)? Why does it matter to their business? Who else is involved? And what should happen in the next conversation?

Before You Hand Off

Before creating the SAO, confirm the qualification standard in Section 16 is met — that's not re-checked here. What this section cares about is different: whether the record and the note actually communicate what you learned, not whether the lead was qualified in the first place. The difference shows up in the notes an AE reads. "Interested in Trimble software, wants a demo" tells them nothing. The Cheyenne example above tells them who they're meeting, what's broken, and why it matters — that's the bar for a good handoff, and it's a different bar than the one for qualifying the lead.

Step-by-Step: From Qualified Lead to Booked Discovery Call

The Gold-Level template and the Five Questions tell you what a good handoff communicates. This is the mechanical process that actually gets you there in Salesforce DX and Google Calendar, once you've decided the lead is ready to become an SAO — the same sequence every SDR should run, end to end.

1. Convert the Lead & Log Your Notes

Before you convert, make sure the lead record is fully filled out — Product of Interest, Contact Role, and anything else required — and put your call notes under the lead's Notes tab prior to conversion. Once that's done, convert the lead to a Contact and create the Opportunity. Follow the SDR Process: Lead to Account/Contact/Opp guide for the click-by-click steps, including how to get a new account approved by Customer Master — or see the full walkthrough with screenshots in Section 21, Tech Stack Workflows.

Copy the note template below directly into a new note on the Opportunity, and fill in every field — this is the raw version of the Gold-Level template above:

Date:
Company:
Address:
Contact (role):
Phone:
Email:
Web:
BANT - Budget, Need, Authority, Timing
Primary Interest (Products):
Users (Scope):
GAR:
Current Software:
Business Need (PAIN):
Next Steps:

Most of this comes straight from Salesforce or from the BANT conversation itself: Date, Company, Address, Contact & Role, Phone, Email, and Web usually live on the record already; Primary Interest, Users, Overall Size, GAR, and Current Software come from Salesforce plus your BANT questions. Business Need, Financial Expectations, and Next Steps have to come directly from the prospect — don't guess at these. Flag anything important the AE needs to know going in: blockers, competitors mentioned, internal dynamics.

If you use an AI-generated summary (a Gong AI Brief, Ask Anything, etc.) as a starting point, add the human insight and nuance the AI is likely to miss before it goes in the note — don't paste it in unedited.
Pro tip: write your notes so the AE could open them and start a relevant conversation without needing to re-ask discovery questions.

2. Create the Opportunity in Salesforce DX

Before converting a lead, confirm you have: Bill-to and Ship-to contact, Net 30, Vertical, Primary industry, Product of interest, Account segment, and Market segment. If you're creating an Amendment Opportunity for an existing customer adding or swapping products, use the separate Amendments in Salesforce DX guide instead.

Additional step-by-step resources from the Salesforce DX Manual: Lead Creation from Salesforce User Interface, Lead Conversion, Manual Account Creation, Opportunity Creation, and the Account Upgrade Process.

Creating the Account is only half the job — it still has to clear Customer Master's sync process before anyone can quote against it. See Section 21's Account Verification walkthrough for the required address, contact, and account-name checks.
Process StepOwner
Create Account & begin Account Upgrade Process, or convert Lead to create AccountSDR
Add a new address to an AccountSDR
Validate/review Account by Customer Master & Sales OpsSales Ops
Assign Territories to AccountSales Ops
Account – Customer Data Hub (CDH) & Oracle syncSales Ops
Validate/confirm sync with Oracle/CDHSales Ops & SDR

Name every Opportunity consistently so downstream reporting and pipeline reviews stay clean:

Company name – Size – Product of Interest – Quarter
Example: Cascade Ironworks – MMNL – Tekla – Q2

3. Schedule the Meeting

Create the invite in Google Calendar and invite the prospect, the AE, and the Product Seller (skip the Product Seller on an ERP opportunity — see the ERP routing exception in Section 22). Before sending, confirm both the AE and Product Seller actually have availability at that time (see this quick video on checking availability in Google Calendar), and double-check you're scheduling in the prospect's time zone, not your own.

Add a brief agenda to the invite's description field, plus the discussion points the prospect wants covered. Two ready-to-adapt agenda examples:

Agenda Example 1 — Open dialogue about [Product]'s features; review of current design processes and how Trimble can better support them; review of licensing options; advantages of establishing a business account; address outstanding questions.
Agenda Example 2 — Welcome & introductions; overview of Trimble solutions; coordinating a demo & discussing next steps.

Once it's booked, transfer ownership of the Google Calendar invite to the AE (More Actions → Change Owner, see below) so they can update the agenda themselves — see the full Transfer events in Google Calendar instructions — and transfer Opportunity ownership in Salesforce to the AE's name. Finally, add your call notes directly onto the Opportunity record.

More actions → Change owner — transfers the calendar invite to the AE so they can update the agenda themselves.

4. Introduce the AE (and Product Seller)

Send a short introduction email right after the call — the goal is a trusted recommendation, not a cold pass-off. Reference what was discussed, name both the AE and Product Seller and what each of them helps with, and confirm the meeting that's already on the calendar.

Hi [Prospect's First Name],

It was a pleasure speaking with you today! As discussed, I wanted to introduce you to a couple of folks from our team who can help take the conversation further:

• [AE Name], your Trimble Account Representative — here to support you with anything related to your broader technology goals.
• [Product Specialist Name], our [Product/Area] expert — available to go deeper on workflows, capabilities, and technical questions.

[1–2 sentences summarizing what was discussed.]

I have scheduled a call for the three of you on [date]. Looking forward to continuing the conversation.

Best regards,
[SDR]

5. Transfer Context & Ownership to the AE

For a complex deal, meet briefly with the AE; otherwise a Google Chat message or Salesforce Chatter note on the Opportunity is enough — as long as the AE can act on it without pinging you first. Make sure the message covers: when the meeting is booked and with whom (name, title, company), a link to the Opportunity in SFDX, where the notes live, and the call notes themselves pasted directly into the message. The AE should walk away knowing what hooked the prospect, where they are in their buying journey, what next step was agreed on, key discussion points, who will attend, what the prospect wants to see or learn, any objections or red flags, and your own recommendations.

"Hi [AE]! I just booked a meeting with [Prospect Name/Title] at [Company] and added you to it. You'll find the call notes here under this opp [link], but I'll paste them here too so you have context right away. Let me know if you need anything else before the meeting."

Check back in to confirm the AE has what they need — reviewed the Opportunity, researched the company, and is following up with the prospect — ideally within 24 hours of the original call. Don't let too much time pass after the initial connect; buyers lose interest fast. If the AE is genuinely delayed, keep the prospect warm yourself with a short message or resource and loop in your manager or the AE directly.

7. AE Follow-Up & 24-Hour Meeting Confirmation

The AE sends their own follow-up email to the prospect ahead of the meeting, referencing your notes and previewing the agenda — this reinforces professionalism and sets expectations before the call. Separately, the SDR sends a short confirmation email 1 business day before the meeting (or the morning of, if it was booked the day prior), CC'ing the AE and Product Seller: a friendly reminder of date, time, and meeting link, a brief recap of what will be covered, and a prompt for any last-minute agenda items.

The morning of the call, give the prospect a quick reminder call as well:

"The day of the meeting I'll give you a ring to serve as a reminder. If I don't hear from you, I will leave a voicemail and shoot over a text. Looking forward to connecting!"

8. Join & Run the Live Handoff on the Discovery Call

Join the meeting 2–3 minutes early to confirm the prospect, AE, and Product Seller have all joined. Best practice is for the SDR to open the call, provide context, and reinforce qualification so the transition to the AE is seamless — a strong live handoff builds credibility with the prospect and prevents the conversation from restarting at zero. In your intro, cover why you connected, the objective for today, the timeframe, and then introduce the AE by name and hand off explicitly.

"Hi [Prospect Name], thanks again for taking the time today... From our earlier conversation, you mentioned [key pain point, initiative, or trigger]. We also talked about [timeline, current tools, or business priority]. The goal for today is to go a level deeper into your current process, understand what success looks like for you, and explore whether it makes sense to continue the conversation... Now that I've set the stage, I'd love to introduce you to [AE Name]. [AE Name] works closely with companies like yours — specifically [industry/segment] — and spends a lot of time helping teams navigate [problem area]. I've shared some of the context for the call today, but they will be your point of contact moving forward. [AE Name], I'll let you take it from here!"

9. If the Prospect No-Shows

TimingAction
Same dayAE calls the prospect and sends a follow-up email, and must let the SDR know the meeting was a no-show. If the SDR booked the meeting by phone, they should have already told the prospect to expect a day-of reminder call.
Next daySDR calls and emails the prospect with 2–3 new time options, copying the AE and Product Seller.
48 hours laterIf there's still no reply, SDR sends a value-add follow-up (a relevant case study, article, or resource) to re-engage, and updates the Salesforce activity log to track every outreach attempt.

10. Post-Handoff Ownership, Feedback & Credit AlignmentSDR + AE

SDRs are responsible for reviewing their own SAO-status opportunities weekly and following up with AEs on meeting outcomes and progression — don't wait for the AE to volunteer an update.

"Hey, how did the meeting with ABC Contracting go? Anything else you need from me before moving forward?"

On the AE side, the opportunity should move to the Discovery stage within 48 hours of the meeting occurring. If the AE creates an opportunity an SDR originally sourced, the SDR's name goes in the Created By field, and the AE updates Close Date and Amount to reflect what was actually discussed on the call.

If the opportunity doesn't move forward but the SDR completed everything required for credit (notes documented, BANT-qualified, meeting occurred), the Loss Reason should be set to Sales Disqualified Opportunity — this keeps the loss off the AE's Seller Scorecard and loss ratio, and still gets the SDR SQO credit. The AE is responsible for logging the loss details in Salesforce and giving specific, structured, actionable meeting-quality feedback (including any qualification gaps) — ideally shared over Google Chat in addition to Salesforce, so it actually gets read.

Set Up the AE Meeting, Not Just the Calendar Invite

A common miss is booking the meeting without explaining why it's worth the customer's time, which is a quiet driver of no-shows. A short line does the work: "I'll connect you with one of our specialists who can go deeper on your workflow and how teams like yours are approaching this."

Staying in Sync With Your AE Pod

Handoff quality isn't a one-time event — it's a feedback loop. A regular cadence with your AE pod (a weekly 1:1, a pipeline review, an occasional strategy sync on target accounts) is where you find out whether your SAOs are landing well before it shows up as a trend in the numbers. If an AE tells you a lead wasn't qualified, or had to redo discovery you thought you'd covered, treat it as a specific, fixable gap — not a verdict on the lead.

What Undermines a Handoff

  • Booking blind — a meeting with no context forces the AE to start from zero.
  • Overpromising — setting an expectation the AE can't actually deliver on.
  • Skipping the "why it matters" — documenting the problem but not its business impact, so the conversation stays stuck on features.
  • Treating the AE as a drop-off point — the handoff is a partnership, not the end of your involvement.

23New Logo SDR Plays

Seven repeatable plays for finding and engaging net-new logo opportunities.

1. Closed-Lost Re-engagement

Just because a company said "no" or "not right now" 6–12 months ago doesn't mean it's a permanent no.

Trigger: A deal that went Closed-Lost 6+ months ago due to "Timing," "Budget," or "Lost to Competitor."
Strategy: Research what's changed since the last conversation — a new decision-maker, new funding, a product release that solves the exact reason they dropped out.

"When we spoke last year, [Previous Pain Point] was a roadblock, and the timing wasn't right. I'm reaching out because we just launched [New Feature/Solution] which specifically solves that, and I wanted to see if priorities have shifted for 2026."

Building your personal Closed-Lost playbook: open the master shell template (SFDX Closed Lost Report — Shell for SDRs), click "Save As" to create your own editable version, then tailor the filters — update Opportunity Owner Names to your current AEs, your name, and any previous SDRs who worked your territory, and adjust the Close Date filter to isolate accounts that went cold 6–12 months ago, the re-engagement sweet spot.

Look closely at the "Lost Reason" notes on old deals. A prospect who suffered "severe software fatigue" or a "budget freeze" last year is a great candidate for a fresh, workflow-driven conversation today.

2. Champion Tracking

The lowest-hanging fruit in outbound: a buyer who already loves Trimble but just switched jerseys.

Trigger: A power-user, champion, or economic buyer from an existing customer leaves their company and takes a job at a new logo account.
Strategy: Use LinkedIn Sales Navigator alerts on "Past Company" filters. When a champion moves to a non-customer company, target them immediately — they already know, trust, and love the product.

"Congrats on the new role at [New Company]! I loved working with you over at [Old Company] to help scale their operations. I'd love to sync for 15 minutes to show you what we're working on now, and see if we can help you make a quick impact in your first 90 days here."

3. Executive Job Changes

A new VP or C-level hire usually comes with a mandate for transformation and fresh budget allocation.

Trigger: A decision-maker persona (VP of Operations, CIO) has been in role less than 90 days (via Sales Nav or ZoomInfo Scoops).
Strategy: Reach out during the onboarding window (days 30–90), when they're actively auditing existing processes and looking for modern tools to prove their value to the board.

"Congrats on taking the reins of the Operations team. Typically, when new leadership steps into a role like yours, mapping out data silos and field efficiency is top of mind. Here is how we helped [Similar Peer Company] optimize their workflow during a similar transition…"

4. Competitor Contract Window Play

Time your outreach to hit right as a competitor's contract comes up for renewal.

Trigger: ZoomInfo technographic data shows a target account using a direct competitor, combined with manual research suggesting they've had that tool roughly 1–2 years (standard contract length).
Strategy: Start multi-threading 90–120 days before the suspected renewal date — waiting until 30 days out means they're already locked in.

"I see you are currently utilizing [Competitor] for your fleet management. A lot of companies we talk to switching over to us are experiencing [Common Competitor Flaw/Pain Point]. Since you might be evaluating your stack ahead of your next renewal cycle, I wanted to share…"

5. Intent Data Play

Instead of guessing who's in-market, look at who's actively researching your category.

Trigger: A target account shows a spike in intent data (ZoomInfo or Bombora) for keywords like "BIM software compliance" or "telematics integration."
Strategy: Don't say "I saw you searching for us." Treat the data as a smoke signal — if there's smoke, there's fire. Drop 3–4 personas from that company into a highly relevant, problem-centric sequence immediately.

"A lot of [Job Titles] I speak with right now are struggling to bridge the gap between their field hardware data and office SaaS metrics. We actually just put together a framework on how to solve this…"

6. Reverse-Engineering a Good Account From Closed-Won Opportunities

Look at who already gave Trimble money, figure out why, and go find their lookalikes.

  • Closed-Won audit: extract the DNA of 3–5 accounts in your territory that closed in the last 6 months — size (revenue/headcount), exact vertical niche (heavy highway vs. utility), and current tech stack.
  • "Good account" checklist: a high-probability civil account usually has high asset density (lots of heavy equipment), an active public bid profile (winning DOT or infrastructure contracts), and a "digital gap" (strong office engineers but manual paper/stakes in the field). Look for NAICS codes 237310 (Highway, Street, and Bridge) or 238910 (Site Preparation).
  • Clone them: in ZoomInfo, take your closed-won list and hit "Generate Lookalikes." In Sales Navigator, go to a successful customer's company page, scroll to "Similar Companies," and harvest the 5–10 peer accounts LinkedIn suggests.

7. Marketing Prioritized Leads (MPLs) Play

MPLs represent demonstrated interest — a webinar attendee, a whitepaper download. This play is about speed-to-lead: striking while the iron is hot, before warm inbound intent cools down.

Trigger: A high-intent MPL is generated from marketing engagement and assigned to you.
Strategy: Speed and consistent tracking are the priority. You have a strict 1-business-day window to make first touch, which secures an exclusive 3-day ownership protection window. Before logging any outreach, officially claim and reassign the lead to yourself in Salesforce — and once claimed, ignore territory boundaries entirely and work it immediately.

"Hi [Name], I noticed you were recently checking out our resources regarding [Specific Marketing Topic/Asset]. A lot of [Job Titles] I speak with who look into this are trying to bridge the gap between their field operations and office SaaS metrics. I'd love to sync for 10 minutes to show you how we helped [Similar Peer Company] optimize their workflow in this exact area…"

MPL rules of engagement:

  • Claim before you contact — you can't log activity or start outreach until the lead is officially reassigned to you in Salesforce.
  • The 24-hour clock — documented outreach (call, email, LinkedIn touch, or a Gong Flow) must start within 1 business day of assignment.
  • Use it or lose it (the 3-day rule) — if an MPL sits 3 consecutive calendar days with no documented Salesforce activity, protection is automatically forfeited and it's open season for a teammate to claim.
  • Ignore territory borders — marketing data isn't always aligned to patches; pursue and book meetings from any MPL assigned to you regardless of geography, vertical, or account ownership. Speed-to-lead overrides territory rules, and you get full credit for the opportunity.
Turn your peers' forgotten leads into your pipeline. Routinely audit Salesforce for inactive, unworked MPLs that have crossed the 3-day threshold — if abandoned, reassign to yourself, log your first touch, and pick up a warm opportunity someone else left on the table.

24AI for Outbound SDRs

Outbound requires balancing two things in tension: personalization deep enough to matter, and enough efficiency to cover a real territory. Enterprise and Mid-Market accounts demand real understanding of the company, the industry, the role, and the timing — more than a quick glance can provide. AI's job is closing that gap: research faster, draft better first passes, prepare more thoroughly, all without the SDR skills that actually create relationships (curiosity, judgment, listening) going anywhere. The goal was never "send more emails faster" — it's "create more relevant conversations with the right customers." Treat every output as a first draft, always add real context to your prompts (company, industry, persona, challenge, desired outcome all sharpen the result), and check anything before it goes out: is this accurate, relevant, and does it actually sound like a person wrote it?

Where AI Helps

Use CaseWhat It Helps WithExample Prompt
Account researchCompany overview, business initiatives, likely challenges before you ever reach out"Analyze [Company]. Include company overview, industries served, business model, growth signals, strategic initiatives, and potential reasons Trimble AECO solutions may be relevant."
Prospect researchUnderstanding a specific person's likely priorities and concerns based on role"Analyze this LinkedIn profile for an outbound conversation. Summarize likely responsibilities, business priorities, potential challenges, and relevant discovery questions."
Persona messagingAdjusting the angle of a message for executive, operations, or technical audiences"Create outbound messaging for a VP-level executive at a construction company, focused on business outcomes and strategic priorities."
Email generationA relevant first draft built on real account research, not a generic template"Write a personalized outbound email to [Persona] at [Company] using this research: [insert]. Focus on a relevant challenge, create curiosity, end with a simple question."
Call planningAn opening, likely challenges, discovery questions, and anticipated objections"Help me prepare for a call with [Company] and [Contact]. Provide a recommended opening, likely challenges, discovery questions, and possible objections."
Competitive researchUnderstanding how Trimble compares without resorting to unverified claims"Compare [Competitor] and Trimble for a construction organization — customer challenges, workflow differences, business outcomes, conversation points."
Executive summariesA fast brief for AEs, leadership, or specialists joining a strategic account"Create an executive account summary: company overview, strategic priorities, potential challenges, key stakeholders, recommended messaging, next steps."
Territory analysisSpotting trends and prioritization opportunities across an assigned segment"Analyze my territory of [industry/geography]. Identify major trends, common challenges, potential buying triggers, and recommended account prioritization."

On competitive research specifically: use it to have a more informed conversation, never to attack a competitor or repeat an unverified claim externally. Always validate before it leaves your hands.

A Simple AI-Assisted Workflow

Research the account and summarize company, industry, and business signals. Identify the relevant personas and their likely priorities. Draft outreach — email, call opening, LinkedIn message. Prepare for the actual conversation with discovery questions and anticipated objections. Afterward, summarize what you learned back into your account intelligence. AI can support every step; you're still the one deciding what's actually true and relevant.

Guardrails

Always verify facts AI generates before repeating them to a customer — it can be confidently wrong. Never enter confidential customer information into a tool that isn't Trimble-approved for that data. And keep the voice yours: AI should sharpen what you'd say, not replace your judgment or the relationship-building that actually creates results. Technology accelerates a good SDR. It doesn't replace one.

PART VI

Measuring Success

25Metrics

Metrics aren't a number to hit — they're signals about what's actually working. The best SDRs don't ask "how do I hit my activity goal," they ask "which activities create the highest-quality conversations with the right customers." A hundred generic emails will almost always produce fewer real opportunities than twenty-five highly personalized conversations with strategic accounts — so the goal was never maximum activity. It's the right activity, with the right accounts, using the right message, at the right time.

Five Categories

Outbound performance breaks down into activity (what's being done), engagement (are prospects responding), conversion (are activities becoming conversations and opportunities), pipeline impact (is any of this contributing to revenue), and quality (are we creating the right opportunities, not just more of them). Activity is the input; the other four determine whether it actually turns into anything.

Daily Activity Goals

These are the baseline activity numbers the daily schedule in Section 20 is built to produce — a floor to hit consistently, not a ceiling to stop at once you've reached it.

MetricTarget
Dials60
Conversations6–8
Meetings Set1
Emails Sent30–60
New Accounts Prospected5+

If dials are on target but conversations aren't, that's a connect-rate problem (contact data, timing) rather than an effort problem — see the diagnostic table below. If conversations are healthy but meetings aren't, that's usually a discovery or relevance issue, not a volume one.

Quotas & Standing Expectations

Beyond the daily numbers above, a handful of metrics get tracked on a longer horizon:

MetricExpectation
SAOs & SQOsQuota
Pipeline GeneratedQuota
Activities (calls, emails, and LinkedIn touches, tracked separately) per day, week, period, and quarterUse your individual conversion rates to back into how many dials you personally need to hit your SQO quota — the Dial Calculator Spreadsheet does the math for you
Prospects currently in flow~75–150 is standard
Lead Qualification Rate10% (industry standard)
Engagement Rate10% (industry standard)

The dial and email/LinkedIn targets in the Daily Activity Goals table above are the specific per-channel floor; this is the roll-up view your manager is actually watching over a longer window.

Engagement Metrics

MetricFormulaA Weak Number Usually Means
Connect RateSuccessful connections ÷ outreach attemptsBad contact data, poor call timing, or targeting that isn't landing
Conversation RateMeaningful conversations ÷ outreach attemptsA connection isn't the same as a conversation — weak opening, irrelevant messaging, or wrong persona
Meeting RateMeetings booked ÷ conversationsDiscovery isn't creating enough relevance or customer curiosity to advance
Positive Reply RatePositive responses ÷ total outreachPersonalization, targeting, or value proposition isn't landing (see Section 15 for messaging fundamentals)

Sequence performance rolls several of these up over time — completion rate, reply rate by step, and channel effectiveness. The useful questions: which step in the sequence creates the most engagement, which channel performs best, where do prospects consistently drop off, and what does that imply about the messaging at that point?

Opportunity Metrics

Section 22 already covers what makes a quality SAO and the checklist for creating one — the metric version is simply how many you're creating and at what acceptance rate. An SQO (Sales Qualified Opportunity) is the next stage: an opportunity that's passed the AE's own qualification standards and is actively progressing through the sales process. The SAO → SQO conversion rate is one of the most useful diagnostics available — a high SAO volume with a low SQO rate almost always points back to qualification quality, not effort.

Pipeline & ACV Contribution

Pipeline contribution is the potential revenue tied to opportunities you've created or influenced — the actual link between your daily activity and future business impact. ACV (Annual Contract Value) contribution weights that further: not every opportunity is worth the same, and an SDR working Enterprise accounts should weigh account value and strategic importance, not just count.

Reading the Conversion Chain

Opportunities move through a consistent chain: activity → conversation → meeting → SAO → SQO → pipeline. Where the chain breaks tells you what to fix.

PatternLikely Cause
High activity, low meetingsMessaging, targeting, or both aren't landing
High meetings, low SQOsMeeting quality or qualification rigor, not volume
High SAOs, low SQO conversionOpportunities are being created before they're actually qualified

Territory Penetration & Account Coverage

Territory penetration — the percentage of target accounts actually contacted, and how many have active engagement — is the coverage check on the account prioritization work in Sections 9 and 10. A territory can't generate pipeline if priority accounts are sitting untouched. Account coverage is the same idea one level deeper: for Mid-Market and Enterprise accounts specifically, one contact is rarely enough (Section 11's multi-threading guidance applies directly here) — strong coverage means decision-makers, influencers, users, and technical stakeholders, not just whoever answered first.

Quality, Underneath the Numbers

Quantity creates opportunities; quality creates pipeline. Worth checking regularly: does the account actually fit the ICP, are you engaging the right personas, is there a real business challenge behind the activity, is the prospect actively participating rather than just responding politely, and is the opportunity continuing to move rather than stalling.

Review Rhythm

Daily: completed activities, priority follow-ups, engagement from the day. Weekly: conversations created, meetings booked, account progress, pipeline impact. Monthly: conversion trends, territory coverage, and whether messaging needs to adjust. Each cadence answers a different question — daily is "did I execute," weekly is "is it working," monthly is "what should change."

Where Metrics Get Misused

MistakeBetter
Focusing only on activity volumeBalance activity against actual conversion and quality
Ignoring conversion rates between stagesAnalyze where prospects actually move or drop off
Measuring meetings instead of pipelineA meeting isn't the outcome — a meaningful opportunity is

The SDR Scorecard

CategoryExamples
ActivityCalls, emails, LinkedIn engagement
EngagementConnect rate, conversation rate, positive replies
MeetingsMeetings created, meeting quality
OpportunitiesSAOs, SQOs
PipelinePipeline created, ACV contribution
TerritoryAccount coverage, penetration
QualityConversion rates, opportunity progression
DevelopmentTraining completed, coaching actions applied, skill improvement

The goal was never more activity for its own sake. It's the right accounts engaged, the right conversations created, the right opportunities generated — and pipeline that actually reflects it.

26Performance Excellence

Great SDRs aren't created by activity alone — they're created by continuous improvement. Average performers wait for feedback and ask what their manager is looking for. High performers seek feedback out and ask what they can do to get better. The goal was never perfection. It's progress, applied consistently.

The Growth Loop

Execute (complete the activities, engage the customer), measure (review the actual results), reflect (understand what worked and what didn't), adjust (change the behavior, message, or strategy), and repeat. It's a simple cycle, but most of the value is in actually closing the loop — skipping the reflect step is the most common way this breaks down.

Self-Coaching

The ability to evaluate your own performance is one of the strongest predictors of long-term success in this role, mostly because you spend far more time executing independently than you do with your manager. The shift is small but real: instead of asking "did this work," ask "what did I learn." After a call, email, or meeting, three questions are usually enough — what went well, what could improve, and what will I actually do differently next time. A few sharper prompts by category: on messaging, did it focus on the customer's priorities and create real curiosity? On conversations, did I listen more than I talked, and did I actually uncover a business challenge? On execution, did I prioritize the right accounts and follow up on what I said I would?

Reviewing Your Own Calls

Section 21 covers what Gong is for at a high level; this is how to actually use it for self-improvement. The point of reviewing your own calls isn't to criticize yourself — it's to find specific, fixable moments. Listen for the opening (did it create interest quickly and land as relevant), the flow (strong questions, or a slide into pitching too early), customer engagement (did they participate, or did you carry the whole conversation), and the next step (was it clear, and did the customer have a reason to want it).

A useful documentation format after a review: what worked (specifically — "the industry-specific opening created engagement because the prospect immediately recognized the challenge"), one opportunity to improve ("I could have asked more about the impact of the current process"), and one concrete action ("in my next five calls, I'll ask at least three discovery questions before mentioning a solution"). Vague takeaways don't change behavior; specific ones do.

Inspecting Your Own Pipeline

Pipeline health isn't only an AE's job to track. Section 25 covers the metrics themselves; the questions worth asking yourself regularly are about the story behind them — are you engaging the right accounts and reaching enough stakeholders within them, is there a real business challenge and genuine customer engagement behind what's in your pipeline, and are conversations actually progressing into meetings, SAOs, and beyond, or stalling at a predictable point.

Reading Your Scorecard

Section 25 has the full scorecard structure. Beyond "did I hit my number," it's worth asking what behaviors actually drove the good weeks, what patterns show up across your data, where your biggest single opportunity for improvement sits, and what one skill would move the needle most if you focused on it next.

Where to Keep Improving

A 1% improvement compounds fast when it's daily rather than occasional. Worth developing deliberately: prospecting skills (research, messaging, personalization), communication (listening, questioning, confidence), business acumen (industry knowledge, market awareness), and core sales skills (qualification, discovery, objection handling).

Building a Development Plan

A plan worth keeping covers four things: your actual strengths (what you're already doing well), the growth area that would move the needle most, specific actions (reviewing five Gong calls, shadowing an AE discovery call, practicing a specific messaging framework, completing a training module), and how you'll know it worked (a higher conversion rate, better conversations, more confidence — something you can actually observe).

Getting the Most From Manager Coaching

Coaching works best as a two-way conversation, not a one-way review. Managers typically coach across three areas: strategy (territory planning, account prioritization), skill (messaging, calls, discovery, objections), and performance (metrics, behaviors, improvement plans). It goes further when you show up prepared — bring actual data ("my connect rate has dropped over the last month"), a real observation ("prospects seem to engage more when I lead with industry challenges"), and a specific question ("what would you change about my opening?") rather than waiting to be told what to work on.

Where Performance Stalls

MistakeBetter
Relying only on activity volumeAnalyze quality and conversion alongside it
Avoiding feedbackSeek it out proactively — growth slows without it
Repeating the same approach despite flat resultsTest something different, then learn from it
Measuring only outcomes, which lagFocus on the controllable behaviors that drive them

The SDRs who become top performers aren't the ones who never make mistakes — they're the ones who learn faster, adjust quicker, and keep raising their own bar without waiting to be told to.

27Appendix

Quick-reference material that pairs with the chapters above — templates, question banks, and checklists meant to be scanned in the moment rather than read start to finish. Where something here overlaps with a full chapter, it points back there instead of repeating it.

AProspecting Frameworks

Section 15 covers the reasoning behind each of these; this is the compressed, fill-in-the-blank version for when you're mid-sequence and need the shape of the message fast.

Cold Call

1. Intro: "Hi [Name], this is [Your Name] with Trimble. I know I'm calling unexpectedly — do you have 30 seconds for why I reached out?"
2. Relevance: "I work with organizations in [industry] looking to improve [outcome]. I noticed [observation], and wanted to see if that's something your team is focused on."
3. Curiosity: "A lot of [industry] leaders are looking at ways to improve [challenge] — curious how your team's approaching that today."
4. Discovery question: "How are you currently managing that process?"
5. Next step: "Sounds like there may be something worth exploring — would it make sense to put time on the calendar with one of our specialists?"

Do: sound confident, stay curious, ask questions, listen, create value. Avoid: reading a script verbatim, pitching immediately, talking too much, forcing a meeting.

Email: Problem → Insight → Question

Subject: short and specific — "Improving [workflow]," "Question about [initiative]"

Opening (why them): "I noticed [company initiative/trend/change]. Many organizations in [industry] are evaluating ways to improve [challenge]."
Insight (why reach out): "Teams we work with are often looking for better ways to improve visibility, reduce inefficiencies, and create more connected workflows."
Question: "How is your team currently approaching this?" / "Would it be worth comparing notes?"

Voicemail (under 30 seconds)

"Hi [Name], this is [Your Name] with Trimble. I'm reaching out because we work with organizations in [industry] focused on [challenge]. I wanted to share a few ideas on how companies are approaching that. I'll send a quick note as well — my info is [info]. Look forward to connecting."

LinkedIn

Connection request: "Hi [Name], I work with organizations in the [industry] space and noticed your work at [Company]. I'd enjoy connecting and following the initiatives your team is focused on."

After connecting: "Thanks for connecting, [Name]. I've been following some of the work happening in [industry]. Curious how your team is approaching [challenge]."

Sample Multi-Channel Cadence

DayTouchPurpose
1Email + CallIntroduce relevance
3Call + LinkedIn engagementBuild familiarity
5EmailShare additional value
8CallAttempt conversation
12Break-up or timing emailCreate a final opening to engage

(Section 18 has the fuller channel-strategy version of this, including how the mix shifts by account tier.)

BDiscovery Questions

A question bank to pull from — Section 16 covers discovery philosophy and flow in depth. The core discipline either way: current state → challenges → impact → future state → next step.

By Persona

PersonaFocusQuestions
ExecutiveStrategy, growth, risk"What are the biggest priorities for your organization this year?" "How are you measuring success in this area?" "What could prevent you from reaching those goals?"
OperationsEfficiency, workflow"How are your teams currently managing this workflow?" "What processes require the most manual effort?" "Where do teams lose visibility today?"
Project LeadersExecution, delivery"Where do projects typically experience delays?" "How do teams communicate changes today?" "What information is hardest to access when making decisions?"
TechnicalSystems, integration"How well do your systems work together today?" "Where do users experience friction?" "What capabilities matter most when evaluating technology?"

By Industry

IndustryQuestions
Civil"How are your field and office teams staying connected today?" "What challenges do you experience managing project data?"
MEP"How does your team currently manage coordination across disciplines?" "Where do projects experience the most rework?"
General Contracting"How do you currently manage project information across teams?" "How are you measuring project performance?"
Structures"How does your team manage complex project requirements?" "Where do you experience challenges coordinating information?"
ERP Cross-Sell"How has your current Trimble solution supported your team?" "Are there workflows outside your current solution where you see opportunities?"

The Underlying Structure

Current state ("What are you doing today?") → challenges ("What isn't working as well as you'd like?") → impact ("How does that affect your business?") → future state ("What would you like to improve?") → next step ("Would it make sense to explore how others are addressing this?"). Every question bank above is really this structure applied to a specific audience.

Persona Research

PromptPurpose
"Analyze the role of a [Job Title] at a [Industry] company: responsibilities, priorities, common challenges, success metrics, and what outcomes matter most to them."Understanding a specific role
"For a [Company Type] evaluating construction technology, identify likely buying-process stakeholders — executives, business leaders, technical users, influencers — and potential concerns for each."Building a stakeholder map
"What challenges does a [Job Title] typically experience related to [workflow]? Provide messaging angles and discovery questions."Persona-specific messaging

Executive Preparation

PromptPurpose
"Create an executive briefing for a conversation with [Name], [Title] at [Company]: likely priorities, strategic initiatives, industry challenges, talking points, and questions that create a strategic conversation."Prepping for senior stakeholders
"Help me prepare for an executive-level conversation, focused on business outcomes and strategic priorities rather than product."Avoiding a product-led pitch at the wrong altitude

Email

PromptPurpose
"Write a personalized outbound email to [Name], [Title] at [Company] using this research: [insert]. Concise, focused on a relevant challenge, ends with a simple question."First-touch email
"Create an outbound email for a [industry] leader focused on [challenge]. Goal is curiosity, not a pitch — industry language, consultative tone."Industry-specific messaging
"Rewrite this email to be more customer-focused, relevant, and personalized — reduce generic language and strengthen the reason to respond."Improving a draft
"Write a concise executive outreach email to a [Title] at [Company], focused on strategic priorities and business outcomes, not features."Executive-level email

Call Planning & Review

PromptPurpose
"Help me prepare for a cold call with [Contact] at [Company]: recommended opening, relevant challenges, discovery questions, likely objections, and a next step."Pre-call prep
"Create discovery questions for a [Job Title] at a [Industry] company, focused on current process, challenges, impact, and desired future state."Discovery prep
"Review this call summary and identify what went well, areas to improve, missed discovery opportunities, and recommendations for next time."Self-coaching (see Section 26)

Objection Handling

PromptPurpose
"Help me respond to this objection: '[Objection]'. Acknowledge the concern, ask a thoughtful follow-up, and keep the conversation moving."Real-time response prep
"Analyze this objection and explain what may be behind it — possible reasons, follow-up questions, and recommended responses."Understanding root cause

Meeting Summaries & Handoffs

PromptPurpose
"Summarize this customer conversation: goals, challenges, current process, pain points, stakeholders, qualification info, next steps."Fast post-call notes
"Create an AE handoff summary from these SDR notes: account background, challenge, business impact, stakeholders, conversation history, expectations, recommended meeting objective."Handoff prep (see Section 22)

Territory Analysis

PromptPurpose
"Analyze my territory of [industry/geography]: major companies, market trends, common challenges, buying triggers, and account prioritization recommendations."Territory planning
"Analyze this territory for white space opportunities, considering company size, industry fit, growth signals, and technology adoption."Finding untapped accounts (Section 11)
"Create an account prioritization framework for these companies, ranked by ICP fit, business signals, potential need, strategic value, and likelihood of engagement."Ranking a target list

FTemplates & Checklists

Fill-in-the-blank versions of the structures referenced throughout this playbook. Copy into your own notes or Salesforce record as needed.

Account Planning Template

FieldNotes
Company / Industry / Website / HQ / Employees
Current Trimble relationship
Company overview & strategic priorities
Recent news / events / growth signals
Industry trends & common challenges
Potential business drivers

Stakeholder map:

ContactRoleInfluencePriorityNotes

Opportunity hypothesis: potential challenges, potential Trimble alignment, reason to engage now.
Outreach strategy: primary personas, messaging approach, channels, next steps.

Meeting Preparation Checklist

Before: research the company and attendees, review previous interactions, understand the industry, identify likely challenges, prepare discovery questions, confirm the meeting objective.
During: capture customer goals, current processes, challenges, business impact, stakeholders, timeline, next steps.
After: update Salesforce, write up customer notes, log follow-up actions, align with your AE, prep for the next meeting.

AE Handoff Template

FieldNotes
Account / Industry / Website / Tier
Primary contact, title, role in decision
Additional stakeholders
Why did the customer engage?
Current situation & business challenges
Desired outcomes
Need / Authority / Current solution / Timeline / Budget
What the customer wants to learn & recommended AE focus
Potential concerns

Salesforce Documentation Checklist

Account records: correct account, industry updated, ownership confirmed, relevant notes captured.
Contact records: info verified, role/persona documented, relationship history captured.
Activity records: calls logged, emails documented, LinkedIn engagement captured, next steps recorded.
Handoff documentation: customer challenge documented, qualification info included, meeting context provided, AE expectations aligned.

The standard, as always (see Section 22): avoid "interested in learning more" — write "Operations leader is exploring ways to improve project visibility due to increasing project complexity and disconnected workflows." Capture the customer's own language where you can, and before moving on, ask whether another seller could actually pick up this account from your notes alone.
